stem: Which of these are health metrics a clinic might record at a checkup? Select all that apply.
options: ["Favorite music genre", "Blood pressure", "Resting heart rate", "Number of social media followers", "Height and weight"]
rationale: Health metrics are measurable facts about the body or habits, like blood pressure, heart rate, and height and weight.

stem: Sort each fictional person's result as a positive health metric or one that needs attention.
options: ["Positive metric", "Needs attention"]
rows: ["Sleeps about 5 hours on school nights", "Blood pressure far above the normal range at repeated visits", "Resting heart rate of 68 beats per minute", "Sleeps 9 hours on most school nights"]
rationale: Positive metrics fall in healthy ranges for a teen; repeated readings outside those ranges are a signal to follow up.

stem: Jamal's blood pressure was a little high at one visit. Which statement about reading health metrics is most accurate?
options: ["Healthy ranges are identical for every person, whatever their age.", "A reading outside the usual range proves that the person is already sick.", "One number always shows the full picture of a person's overall health.", "One reading is a single data point, and trends over time matter too."]
rationale: Metrics are most useful when tracked over time and interpreted by a professional in context.

stem: Sort each lifestyle factor by whether it generally supports health or diminishes it.
options: ["Supports health", "Diminishes health"]
rows: ["Long stretches of sitting with little movement", "Regularly getting too little sleep", "Regular physical activity", "Eating a variety of fruits and vegetables"]
rationale: Activity and balanced eating support health metrics; inactivity and chronic sleep loss work against them.

stem: Dana (fictional) sleeps 5 hours a night and sits most evenings. Which change would most likely improve her health metrics?
options: ["Drink an energy drink every afternoon to stay awake.", "Stop checking health numbers and simply ignore them.", "Move more during the day and go to bed earlier.", "Skip breakfast so there is more time to sleep in."]
rationale: Regular movement and enough sleep are lifestyle changes that improve many health metrics at once.

stem: Which of these are physical health metrics? Select all that apply.
options: ["Hours of sleep per night", "How well a person handles disappointment", "Minutes of physical activity per day", "Resting heart rate", "How many people they feel close to"]
rationale: Physical metrics measure the body and its habits, such as sleep, heart rate, and activity.

stem: Which is the best example of a mental health metric?
options: ["How well a person can focus and manage stress", "How many steps a person takes in a typical day", "A person's resting blood pressure at a checkup", "How many close friends a person has at school"]
rationale: Mental health metrics describe thinking, focus, stress, and coping rather than the body or relationships.

stem: A fictional student sleeps poorly and then has trouble focusing and feels irritable. What does this show about wellness?
options: ["The dimensions of wellness are connected and affect each other.", "Each dimension of wellness works on its own, separate from the others.", "Mood is only changed by the foods a person eats each day.", "Only physical health affects how well a student does in school."]
rationale: Physical habits like sleep influence mental and emotional wellness, so the dimensions are linked.

stem: Priya (fictional) often feels left out and has no one to talk to when school is hard. Which dimension of wellness is mostly affected?
options: ["Social wellness", "Financial wellness", "Environmental wellness", "Physical wellness"]
rationale: Having supportive relationships and someone to talk to are social wellness metrics.

stem: Sort each example by the dimension it best shows.
options: ["Social wellness", "Emotional wellness"]
rows: ["Notices when feeling overwhelmed and uses a coping skill", "Has at least one trusted person to talk with", "Can name feelings and handle disappointment without lashing out", "Treats others with respect and communicates clearly"]
rationale: Social wellness is about relationships; emotional wellness is about understanding and managing feelings.

stem: What is the main purpose of a personal wellness self-assessment?
options: ["To reflect honestly on current habits and find strengths and areas to improve", "To prove to others that a person is already healthy enough", "To diagnose a medical condition using a short checklist", "To earn a score that gets compared with other students' scores"]
rationale: A self-assessment is a reflection tool; it is not a test, a diagnosis, or a ranking.

stem: Maya's (fictional) self-assessment shows sleep 2 out of 5, physical activity 4 out of 5, and stress 3 out of 5. What are her strength and her area to improve?
options: ["Strength: physical activity. Area to improve: sleep.", "She has no strengths because none of her scores is a 5.", "Strength: stress. Area to improve: physical activity.", "Strength: sleep. Area to improve: physical activity."]
rationale: Her highest score is a strength and her lowest score is the clearest area to work on.

stem: Match each description to the SMART letter it shows.
options: ["Specific", "Measurable", "Achievable", "Relevant", "Time-bound"]
rows: ["Has a deadline: by the end of May", "Realistic for your schedule and resources", "Names exactly what you will do: drink water with lunch", "Includes a number you can track: 20 minutes", "Matters for your own wellness needs"]
rationale: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.

stem: A goal says, "Be healthier." Which revision fixes the missing SMART parts?
options: ["Exercise a lot more and eat much better in the near future.", "Run a full marathon next week, even with no training so far.", "Walk 20 minutes after school on 4 days a week for the next 6 weeks.", "Never eat sweets again, starting tomorrow, for the rest of the year."]
rationale: The revision names the action, a number, a realistic plan, and a time frame.

stem: Which of these goals include all five SMART parts? Select all that apply.
options: ["Sleep 8 hours on school nights, Sunday to Thursday, for the next month to help focus in class.", "Drink 6 cups of water a day for two weeks to reduce afternoon headaches.", "Lose a lot of weight fast.", "Be less stressed."]
rationale: A SMART goal names a specific action, a measure, a realistic target, a reason, and a deadline.

stem: Which are warning signs that a health claim may be misleading? Select all that apply.
options: ["Uses only before-and-after photos and personal testimonials as proof", "Promises fast results with no effort, like \"lose 15 pounds in 10 days\"", "Cites a named study and links to it", "Sells a product while giving the advice", "Is reviewed by a medical organization"]
rationale: Quick-fix promises, testimonials instead of evidence, and a sales motive are common red flags.

stem: Sort each feature by whether it points to a credible source or a source to question.
options: ["Credible source", "Question this source"]
rows: ["An influencer with many followers who sells supplements", "Cites research and names its authors", "Anonymous post with no sources", "A government health agency or university medical center"]
rationale: Credible sources show expertise and evidence; popularity and a sales motive do not make a source credible.

stem: A fitness influencer with millions of followers says a tea "melts belly fat." What does their popularity show?
options: ["Nothing about its truth, because evidence decides credibility.", "The claim must be true, because so many people choose to follow them.", "The claim is true if many comments under the video agree with it.", "The claim is true as long as the influencer looks physically fit."]
rationale: Follower counts and appearance are not evidence; credibility comes from expertise and reliable proof.

stem: Which is the best way to check a health claim you saw on social media?
options: ["Share it widely and see whether most of your friends believe it too.", "Compare it with credible sources like the CDC or NIH.", "Search social media for another post that makes the exact same claim.", "Trust it when the video looks professionally filmed and well edited."]
rationale: Verifying means checking the claim against reliable, independent sources, not repeating it.

stem: A fictional ad claims a supplement "burns fat while you sleep." Which decision and reason are best?
options: ["Do not trust it yet: no evidence is given, and the seller profits from the claim.", "Do not trust it: advertisements are always lies and never true.", "Trust it: the ad is full of five-star customer reviews and photos.", "Trust it: supplements are always tested for safety and results first."]
rationale: A good justification points to missing evidence and the seller's motive, not to reviews or blanket distrust.

stem: Sam (fictional) has a big test tomorrow. It is 11:30 p.m. and friends invite him to play online. What decision must Sam make?
options: ["Whether he should take the test or skip it altogether", "Whether to stay up playing or go to sleep", "Whether his online friends are truly good friends or not", "Which online game would be the most fun to play tonight"]
rationale: The decision is the choice Sam must make now, which affects his rest and his test.

stem: Lena is exhausted, has homework left, and friends want to hang out online. Which are realistic choices she could make? Select all that apply.
options: ["Tell her friends she will connect tomorrow", "Ignore everything and hope it works out", "Stay up all night doing both", "Play online for a short, set time, then stop and go to bed", "Finish homework, then go to bed on time"]
rationale: Good options are realistic and fit her responsibilities; ignoring the situation is not a choice that solves it.

stem: Sort each consequence of regularly staying up very late on school nights.
options: ["Positive consequence", "Negative consequence"]
rows: ["Finishing a game or show you enjoy", "Feeling tired and irritable over time", "More time to relax with friends tonight", "Trouble focusing in class tomorrow"]
rationale: Choices often have short-term benefits and longer-term costs, and both belong in the decision.

stem: Using the STOP steps, which choice is the most responsible for a tired student with a test tomorrow?
options: ["Skip preparing for the test and hope that it goes well.", "Stay up for as long as friends are still online.", "Set a stopping time, finish what is needed, and sleep enough.", "Do whatever an adult says without thinking about the results."]
rationale: A responsible choice considers consequences for health and responsibilities.

stem: Which reasoning best explains why a choice is a responsible health decision?
options: ["It is the one choice that turns out perfect in every way.", "It is what most of my friends are doing at the same time.", "It weighs short- and long-term consequences for my health.", "It is the choice an adult told me to make, no questions asked."]
rationale: Responsible decisions are based on consequences and ownership, not on pleasing others or perfection.

stem: Which statement best defines mental health?
options: ["Another everyday term that simply means mental illness", "The complete absence of any diagnosed mental illness", "Feeling happy and calm every single day of the school year", "A person's emotional and social well-being in daily life"]
rationale: Everyone has mental health; it is part of overall wellness, not just the absence of illness.

stem: Why is mental health better described as a continuum than as "healthy" or "mentally ill"?
options: ["A person is either mentally healthy or mentally ill and stays that way.", "Only people who have a diagnosis fall anywhere on that range.", "People move along a range from thriving to struggling over time.", "Mental health is set at birth and does not change in life."]
rationale: A continuum shows that mental health shifts with experiences, support, and stress.

stem: Which statements are true about what can influence teen mental health? Select all that apply.
options: ["Sleep and daily routines can affect it", "Willpower is the only thing that matters; outside experiences have no effect", "Supportive family and friends can protect it", "It is fixed at birth and nothing can influence it", "Social media experiences can influence it", "Ongoing bullying or conflict can harm it"]
rationale: Family, peers, school, media, and life experiences all influence mental health; willpower alone is not the whole story.

stem: Sort each factor for a fictional teen as a risk factor or a protective factor.
options: ["Risk factor", "Protective factor"]
rows: ["Feeling close to family", "Being bullied at school", "Feeling connected to a school team or club", "Ongoing lack of sleep"]
rationale: Risk factors raise the chance of struggling; protective factors, like connectedness, help buffer stress.

stem: Which of these statements are inaccurate? Select all that apply.
options: ["Stress is always harmful.", "Seeking counseling means someone cannot handle their own problems.", "Mental health can change throughout a person's life.", "A person with a diagnosed mental illness can still function well.", "People with mental illness are always visibly struggling."]
rationale: These myths add stigma; stress can be helpful in small amounts and counseling is a healthy step.

stem: Which fictional student's situation most likely suggests a need for extra support?
options: ["Feels sad for one day after losing an important game", "Feels tired after a very busy week of activities", "Feels nervous the night before a big test at school", "Has avoided friends and struggled to get up for several weeks"]
rationale: Feelings that last for weeks and interfere with daily life go beyond an everyday challenge.

stem: Which could be warning signs that a person needs help? Select all that apply.
options: ["Feeling nervous before a performance", "A sudden drop in schoolwork", "Talking about feeling hopeless", "Wanting some quiet time after a long day", "Pulling away from friends and activities", "Big changes in sleep or appetite"]
rationale: Lasting changes in behavior, mood, and daily functioning are warning signs; occasional nerves are normal.

stem: Which part of the Duration, Intensity, Interference check does each detail show?
options: ["Duration", "Intensity", "Interference"]
rows: ["Worry is so strong it causes panic", "Has not felt like himself for months", "Has felt this way most days for six weeks", "Can no longer focus on homework or go to practice"]
rationale: How long, how strong, and how much it disrupts daily life all help decide the level of concern.

stem: A fictional student shows several warning signs. Which is the most appropriate source of support?
options: ["An anonymous online forum with no moderators", "Waiting to see if it goes away on its own", "A social media influencer's coping video", "A school counselor or another trusted adult"]
rationale: Counselors and trusted adults can assess the situation and connect the student to the right help.

stem: Why should a peer recognize and refer instead of trying to diagnose a friend?
options: ["A friend can diagnose a disorder after reading about it online.", "Warning signs only matter once a professional has diagnosed someone.", "Only professionals can diagnose, so friends notice and connect.", "Naming the exact disorder is the most helpful thing a friend can do."]
rationale: Peers notice and refer; diagnosing is for professionals.

stem: What happens in the body during the basic stress (fight-or-flight) response?
options: ["The body shuts down to rest until the stressor has passed.", "Heart rate and breathing speed up as the body prepares.", "Heart rate and breathing slow down so the body saves energy.", "Only the mind is affected by stress, never the body."]
rationale: The stress response activates the body, and recovery afterward is important.

stem: Sort each coping behavior as generally helpful or potentially harmful.
options: ["Generally helpful", "Potentially harmful"]
rows: ["Slow, controlled breathing", "Talking with a trusted person", "Avoiding responsibilities and doomscrolling", "Using alcohol or drugs to escape"]
rationale: Helpful coping addresses stress or helps the body recover; harmful coping avoids it or adds new risks.

stem: Which are evidence-informed coping strategies? Select all that apply.
options: ["A short walk or other movement", "Avoiding the problem completely", "Progressive muscle relaxation", "Staying up all night to make up for lost time", "Replacing \"I'm going to fail\" with a more realistic thought", "Slow, controlled breathing"]
rationale: Breathing, movement, relaxation, and realistic thinking help; avoidance and lost sleep make stress worse.

stem: Alex (fictional) has a big game tomorrow and feels jittery. Which strategy fits best?
options: ["Controlled breathing and a short walk to calm down", "Staying up late rewatching old games to feel ready", "Skipping practice to avoid feeling any pressure", "Scrolling for hours to avoid thinking about the game"]
rationale: Calming the body fits a stressor that is about nerves; avoidance does not address it.

stem: Which coping plan for a fictional student is the most realistic and complete?
options: ["Handles every problem alone without telling any other person", "Uses the same single strategy every time, whatever the stressor is", "Lists warning signs, strategies, a trusted person, and when to get more help", "Aims to never feel any stress again, starting right now"]
rationale: A realistic plan matches strategies to stressors, includes support, and knows when to get more help.

stem: Which show active listening? Select all that apply.
options: ["Telling a story about your own bigger problem", "Immediately giving advice", "Giving full attention and putting your phone away", "Letting the person finish without interrupting", "Repeating back what you heard to check you understood"]
rationale: Active listening means attention, patience, and checking understanding before offering ideas.

stem: Sort each response to a struggling friend as supportive or dismissive.
options: ["Supportive", "Dismissive"]
rows: ["That sounds really difficult.", "Other people have it worse.", "I'm glad you told me.", "Just get over it."]
rationale: Supportive language validates feelings; dismissive language minimizes them.

stem: After listening to a friend who is struggling, which response best connects them to support?
options: ["\"Post about it online and see what people say.\"", "\"You should just handle it on your own, honestly.\"", "\"I'll fix this for you, so do not worry.\"", "\"Would you talk to the school counselor? I can go with you.\""]
rationale: Offering to connect and accompany a friend to a trusted adult is a safe, supportive step.

stem: A friend asks you to keep a secret. In which situations must you involve a trusted adult? Select all that apply.
options: ["A friend talks about hurting themselves", "A friend says they plan to hurt someone", "A friend is stressed about an upcoming test", "A friend is being hurt or abused", "A friend had an argument with a sibling"]
rationale: Safety comes before secrecy when someone may be hurt.

stem: A friend keeps coming to you with serious struggles. Which statement is accurate?
options: ["A supporter should promise to keep everything secret no matter what.", "If the friend does not improve, it is the supporter's fault.", "Supporting someone means listening and connecting them to help, not treating them.", "A good friend becomes the person's therapist and treats them."]
rationale: Friends are support, not treatment; professionals and trusted adults provide the help.

stem: Which are sources of mental-health support for teens? Select all that apply.
options: ["An anonymous comment section", "An advertisement promising a quick cure", "A school counselor", "The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline", "A primary-care provider", "A trusted parent, coach, or teacher"]
rationale: Counselors, health providers, trusted adults, and crisis lines are reliable supports.

stem: Sort each resource as crisis support or non-crisis support.
options: ["Crisis support", "Non-crisis support"]
rows: ["Calling 911 in an immediate emergency", "Talking with the school counselor about ongoing stress", "Scheduling regular visits with a therapist", "988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline"]
rationale: Crisis resources are for immediate danger; non-crisis resources support ongoing needs.

stem: Which source is most likely to give credible mental-health information?
options: ["An influencer who earns money by selling a supplement", "A government health agency or medical group like the CDC", "An anonymous post written on a public online forum thread", "An ad promising a quick cure for stress and anxiety"]
rationale: Credible information comes from experts and evidence-based organizations.

stem: Noah (fictional) has felt down for weeks but is not in danger. Which resource fits best?
options: ["Calling 911 right away, even though there is no danger", "Waiting until the situation becomes a real emergency before acting", "Taking advice from strangers in an online comment thread", "A school counselor or primary-care provider to plan next steps"]
rationale: Ongoing, non-emergency concerns match counselors and health providers.

stem: Sort each strategy by the barrier to getting help it helps overcome.
options: ["Stigma or embarrassment", "Cost or transportation", "Not knowing where to go"]
rows: ["Ask a trusted adult to help arrange rides or appointments", "Ask the school counselor about free or low-cost options", "Remember that asking for help is common and a sign of strength", "Check the school's resource list to see who to contact"]
rationale: Naming the barrier makes it easier to choose a strategy that works.

stem: Which of these can influence the health of a community? Select all that apply.
options: ["Access to healthcare", "Nothing, because health is decided only by genes", "Access to affordable healthy food", "Nothing, because health is decided only by each person's choices", "Air and water quality", "Safe places to be physically active"]
rationale: Community conditions like air, water, care, food, and safe spaces all shape health alongside personal choices.

stem: Sort each example as an individual health behavior or an environmental influence.
options: ["Individual behavior", "Environmental influence"]
rows: ["Deciding what to eat for lunch", "Whether a grocery store with fresh food is nearby", "Whether safe sidewalks exist on the route to school", "Choosing to walk to school"]
rationale: Behaviors are personal choices; environmental influences are conditions around a person that make choices easier or harder.

stem: Sort each feature of a fictional neighborhood as a risk factor or a protective factor.
options: ["Risk factor", "Protective factor"]
rows: ["A free community health clinic", "No bus service to the clinic", "A park with walking paths", "A busy highway next to the homes"]
rationale: Risk factors raise the chance of poor health outcomes; protective factors support health.

stem: A fictional neighborhood has no grocery store within five miles. How could this condition influence health?
options: ["Residents may struggle to get fresh, affordable food.", "It only affects adults and has no effect on children or teens.", "It has no effect, since food choices are entirely a personal matter.", "It guarantees that every resident there will eventually become seriously ill."]
rationale: Conditions can make healthy choices easier or harder without determining one person's outcome.

stem: Clinics and grocery stores are nearby, but residents lack reliable transportation. Which intervention is the most realistic and best justified?
options: ["Expand a bus route to the clinic and grocery store, since transportation is the barrier.", "Build a second hospital in the area, even though one is already nearby.", "Open a luxury gym downtown, even though no one has asked for one.", "Tell residents to just walk farther, since distance is a personal matter."]
rationale: A good intervention targets the actual barrier identified in the scenario.

stem: Which best describes the difference between healthcare and public health?
options: ["Public health only responds to emergencies such as outbreaks.", "They mean the same thing, so the two terms can be swapped freely.", "Healthcare mainly treats individuals; public health protects whole populations.", "Public health treats individual patients in hospitals; healthcare protects populations."]
rationale: Healthcare focuses on individual patients, while public health works at the population level.

stem: Which are functions of public-health agencies? Select all that apply.
options: ["Performing surgery on individual patients", "Writing prescriptions for each patient", "Promoting vaccination and prevention programs", "Responding to outbreaks", "Preparing for emergencies", "Tracking disease patterns (surveillance)"]
rationale: Surveillance, prevention, outbreak response, and preparedness protect whole communities.

stem: Match each problem to the group most likely to respond.
options: ["Doctor or hospital", "Local health department", "CDC (federal)"]
rows: ["A student needs treatment for an ear infection", "Running vaccination clinics for a county", "Inspecting restaurants after several people in one town get sick", "Tracking a measles outbreak spreading across many states"]
rationale: Individual care goes to providers; local problems go to local departments; multi-state problems involve the CDC.

stem: Match each question to the part of STOP (Source, Timeliness, Objective, Proof) it checks.
options: ["Source", "Timeliness", "Objective", "Proof"]
rows: ["Is the information from a health agency or expert?", "Does it cite data or research?", "Is the creator trying to sell or persuade?", "Is the information current?"]
rationale: STOP helps judge a source's authority, timing, purpose, and evidence.

stem: Data show a higher asthma rate in Neighborhood A than in Neighborhood B. What does the data alone show?
options: ["That the data must be wrong because it differs", "That pollution in Neighborhood A is the cause", "That people in Neighborhood A make worse health choices", "A gap in outcomes, and the cause needs more information."]
rationale: A disparity shows a difference exists; it does not prove why.

stem: Which are common environmental health hazards? Select all that apply.
options: ["UV radiation from the sun", "Drinking water from a tested, safe supply", "Excessive noise", "Extreme heat", "Walking outdoors when air quality is good", "Air pollution"]
rationale: Air pollution, UV, loud noise, and heat can all harm health.

stem: Match each example to hazard, exposure, or risk.
options: ["Hazard", "Exposure", "Risk"]
rows: ["The chance of sunburn or skin damage", "Strong UV radiation from the midday sun", "Water contaminated with lead", "Working outside at noon without sunscreen"]
rationale: A hazard can cause harm, exposure is contact with it, and risk is the likelihood and severity of harm.

stem: One student uses earbuds at low volume for 30 minutes. Another uses them at very high volume for hours every day. Whose hearing risk is higher?
options: ["The same, because both students use earbuds the same way.", "The second: higher volume, longer time, and more frequent exposure raise risk.", "Neither, because listening to music cannot ever harm hearing.", "The first, because lower volume is somehow more damaging to hearing."]
rationale: Risk depends on intensity, duration, and frequency, not just the presence of a hazard.

stem: Today's Air Quality Index (AQI) is 160, which credible guidance labels "Unhealthy." What is the best interpretation?
options: ["Everyone should limit heavy outdoor exertion, and people with asthma need care.", "The AQI only matters for cars and factories, not for people.", "Only people who smoke or vape are affected by the air quality.", "The air is safe for everyone to exercise as hard as they like."]
rationale: At an AQI in the Unhealthy range, everyone may feel effects and sensitive groups are at greater risk.

stem: A soccer tournament is scheduled on a day with poor air quality. Which protective behaviors are realistic? Select all that apply.
options: ["Check the AQI before and during the event", "Take more breaks and watch for symptoms", "Play harder to finish faster", "Ignore the air quality because nothing can be done", "Shorten games or lower the intensity"]
rationale: Risk can be reduced with practical steps even when the hazard cannot be removed.

stem: A fictional sports drink ad uses upbeat pop music, teen athletes, and social media influencers. Who is the intended audience?
options: ["Teenagers and young adults", "Doctors and other health professionals", "Older adults and retirees", "Young children in elementary school"]
rationale: Music, models, and platforms show who the advertiser wants to reach.

stem: Match each ad line to the persuasive technique it uses.
options: ["Social proof", "Celebrity or influencer endorsement", "Scarcity", "Fear"]
rows: ["\"Join the 2 million teens who already switched!\"", "A famous athlete holds the product", "\"Without this, you're falling behind your teammates.\"", "\"Only 50 left. Limited edition!\""]
rationale: Advertisers use proof from the crowd, famous faces, urgency, and fear to persuade.

stem: An ad shows a smiling athlete holding a sugary drink but never states that it improves performance. What is the implied message?
options: ["That it is the cheapest drink available in the store", "That there is no message at all because no claim is stated", "That drinking it will make you athletic and successful", "That it is made with nothing but plain filtered water"]
rationale: Ads can communicate implied messages without making an explicit claim.

stem: Many students believe "everyone stays up past midnight on school nights," but a survey shows most do not. How can this belief affect behavior?
options: ["It only affects people who already disagree with the belief.", "It cannot, because only hard facts ever influence behavior.", "People often copy what seems normal, even if wrong.", "It only matters if the belief happens to be completely true."]
rationale: People often follow what they think is normal, even when they are wrong about it.

stem: A fast-food chain advertises discount meals to teens on many platforms every day. How could the repeated messages affect community health behaviors?
options: ["It only affects people who already liked the product beforehand.", "It guarantees that every single teen will buy the product.", "Repetition has no effect, because people only decide using facts and prices.", "They can make it seem normal and appealing to many people."]
rationale: Repeated exposure can shape norms and choices across a community without determining any one person's decision.

stem: Which is the clearest, most specific community-health problem statement?
options: ["Students' health is not as good as it could possibly be.", "Our community should be much healthier than it currently is.", "Many students here listen at unsafe volumes, risking harm.", "There is a lot of noise in the world around us every day."]
rationale: A clear problem names who is affected and what the harm is.

stem: For the problem of unsafe listening volume at school, which intervention is the most specific and realistic?
options: ["A volume-awareness campaign with posters and a free hearing-screening day", "A general goal to make everyone at the school healthier overall", "A request that students simply care more about their hearing", "A school-wide ban on all music and headphones at every grade"]
rationale: A good intervention is specific, feasible, and linked to the problem.

stem: To get crosswalk lights installed near a school, which is the best audience for an advocacy message?
options: ["The city council, which can decide and fund it", "A group of students who already agree with the request", "A famous celebrity who has no connection to the town", "Anyone who happens to scroll past a social media post"]
rationale: Advocacy targets people with the power to act.

stem: Which is a clear call to action?
options: ["We ask the school board to approve filling stations by next semester.", "We hope that people will think more about hydration.", "Someone should really do something about water here soon.", "Water is important for the health of everyone at school."]
rationale: A call to action names who should do what and by when.

stem: Which could show that a hearing-safety campaign worked? Select all that apply.
options: ["The share of students using volume limits at a follow-up check", "The number of posters printed", "A student survey on listening volume before and after", "How colorful the posters look"]
rationale: Success is measured by changes in behavior or outcomes, not by effort or appearance.

stem: Match each fictional example to tolerance, physical dependence, or addiction.
options: ["Tolerance", "Physical dependence", "Addiction (substance use disorder)"]
rows: ["The body adjusts so the same dose no longer works as well", "Needing larger amounts to get the same effect", "Continuing to use despite repeated harm and loss of control", "A patient takes prescribed pain medicine as directed and has withdrawal symptoms when it stops, with no compulsive use"]
rationale: Tolerance and physical dependence are body adaptations; addiction involves compulsive use despite harm, so they are not the same.

stem: How can psychoactive substances affect brain function or behavior? Select all that apply.
options: ["They can change how brain cells communicate", "They can affect mood and memory", "They always cause permanent damage after one use", "They can impair judgment and coordination", "They affect behavior only when a large amount is used"]
rationale: Substances alter brain signaling and can change judgment, coordination, mood, and memory.

stem: Which statements about substance-use risk are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: ["Many factors together influence risk, such as stress, genetics, and availability", "Supportive family and friends can reduce risk", "Addiction is just a lack of willpower", "Any single risk factor guarantees addiction", "Starting at a younger age raises the risk of problems"]
rationale: Risk comes from many interacting factors; no single factor decides the outcome.

stem: Why can adolescents be more vulnerable to risk-taking?
options: ["Teens are unable to learn from the consequences of their actions.", "Teen brains are fully developed, so risk comes only from choices.", "Impulse control is still developing while the reward system is very active.", "Impulse control matures first while the reward system lags behind."]
rationale: Adolescent brain development makes reward-seeking strong while self-control is still maturing.

stem: Which source is best for supporting a claim about how addiction affects the brain?
options: ["NIDA, the National Institute on Drug Abuse", "A commercial website that is selling a detox product", "A close friend's strong opinion about the topic", "A viral video posted by an anonymous online account"]
rationale: Credible claims are backed by expert, evidence-based organizations.

stem: Why is nicotine especially concerning for teens?
options: ["Teen brains are protected from nicotine's effects until adulthood.", "It is highly addictive and can affect attention in teens.", "Nicotine is only harmful when it comes from burning cigarettes.", "Nicotine only causes problems after many years of daily use."]
rationale: The developing brain is more vulnerable to nicotine's effects and to dependence.

stem: Which are health risks linked to tobacco or vaping? Select all that apply.
options: ["Better focus in the long run", "Effects on attention and learning", "Improved lung capacity", "Nicotine addiction", "Irritation and harm to the lungs", "Cancer risk from toxic chemicals in burned tobacco"]
rationale: Nicotine, aerosol chemicals, and smoke are linked to addiction, lung harm, brain effects, and cancer.

stem: Match each influence to the category it shows.
options: ["Marketing", "Product design or flavors", "Peer norms"]
rows: ["Fruit and candy flavors", "Social media influencers who make vaping look fun", "Believing \"most teens my age vape\"", "Small, sleek devices that are easy to hide"]
rationale: Marketing, flavors and design, and perceived norms all shape youth nicotine use.

stem: Which of these claims are inaccurate? Select all that apply.
options: ["E-cigarette aerosol is just harmless water vapor.", "Nicotine-free means risk-free.", "Burning tobacco creates many toxic chemicals.", "If a product is sold legally, it must be safe for teens.", "Vaping can still expose users to nicotine and other chemicals."]
rationale: Aerosol contains more than water, and legal sale does not mean safe for youth.

stem: Which counter-message is accurate and teen-appropriate?
options: ["\"Everyone who ever vapes will definitely get lung cancer.\"", "\"Vaping will kill you within a week, so never even try it.\"", "\"Vape aerosol can contain nicotine and other chemicals. Check the CDC.\"", "\"Vaping is totally fine as long as you only do it sometimes.\""]
rationale: Good counter-messages are accurate, avoid exaggeration, and point to credible sources.

stem: Which are short-term effects of alcohol that can affect safety or decisions? Select all that apply.
options: ["Reduced coordination", "Memory problems or blackouts", "Slower reaction time", "Better driving ability", "Sharper decision-making", "Poorer judgment"]
rationale: Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant that impairs judgment, reaction time, coordination, and memory.

stem: Which statements explain why alcohol affects people differently? Select all that apply.
options: ["Everyone is affected the same way by the same number of drinks", "Body size and composition can change the effect", "Feeling fine means a person is not impaired", "Drinking quickly increases impairment compared with drinking slowly", "Food and medications can change the effect"]
rationale: Impairment varies with amount, speed, body, food, and medications, and people cannot reliably judge their own impairment.

stem: A fictional teen's ride home has been drinking. Match each statement to the decision-making step it shows.
options: ["Define the problem", "List options", "Think about consequences", "Choose the safest decision"]
rows: ["I could call a parent, find a sober driver, or stay overnight", "A crash could cause injury, legal trouble, and harm to others", "My ride has been drinking and I need to get home", "I will call a parent for a ride"]
rationale: A structured process moves from the problem to options, consequences, and the safest choice.

stem: Mia (fictional) is offered a ride from someone who has been drinking. Which response best weighs alternatives and consequences?
options: ["Compares options like a sober driver, weighs the risks, and picks the safest", "Avoids making any decision and hopes it all works out fine", "Takes the first ride offered because it is the easiest option", "Decides based on whatever most of the friends there are doing"]
rationale: Safer alternatives and their consequences should be compared before acting.

stem: Which are signs that someone who drank alcohol needs emergency help right away? Select all that apply.
options: ["Being loud and talkative", "Cannot be woken up", "Vomiting repeatedly and confused", "Slow or irregular breathing", "Feeling slightly dizzy but walking and talking normally"]
rationale: Unresponsiveness and breathing problems can mean alcohol poisoning; call emergency services.

stem: Which are ways marijuana can affect functioning or safety? Select all that apply.
options: ["Slower reaction time", "Reduced coordination while driving", "Poorer judgment", "It is harmless because it is natural", "Trouble with attention and memory", "It improves driving reaction time"]
rationale: Cannabis can impair attention, reaction time, coordination, memory, and judgment.

stem: Sort each example as prescribed use or misuse.
options: ["Prescribed use", "Misuse"]
rows: ["Taking medicine exactly as directed by the prescriber", "Taking a friend's ADHD medication to study", "Using a medicine that was prescribed to you, in the amount and way directed", "Taking extra pills because the pain feels worse"]
rationale: Using someone else's medication, more than prescribed, or for another purpose is misuse.

stem: Why can opioids cause life-threatening overdose?
options: ["They only affect people who misuse them regularly.", "They slow breathing, and too much can stop it.", "They speed up the heart until it stops.", "They only cause overdose when injected."]
rationale: Opioids depress breathing, which is what makes overdose life-threatening.

stem: A classmate offers a pill said to be "the same as a prescription one." Why can't that claim show the pill is safe?
options: ["Pills with natural-sounding ingredients are guaranteed to be safe.", "Pills sold for a low price are always the weaker versions.", "Pills that look like medicine always come from drug companies.", "Counterfeit pills can look real but contain fentanyl, so looks prove nothing."]
rationale: You cannot tell what is in a pill by looking, and counterfeit pills can be deadly.

stem: Which are key parts of responding to a suspected opioid overdose? Select all that apply.
options: ["Call 911 right away", "Stay with the person until help arrives", "Give them coffee or food to wake them up", "Give naloxone if it is available", "Wait to see if they sleep it off"]
rationale: Naloxone can temporarily reverse an overdose, but emergency medical help is still needed.

stem: Sort each fictional situation as direct or indirect pressure.
options: ["Direct pressure", "Indirect pressure"]
rows: ["Your ride depends on someone who has been drinking", "A friend says, \"Just try it, don't be weird.\"", "Everyone in the room is holding a vape", "Someone keeps handing you a drink and asking again"]
rationale: Direct pressure is said out loud; indirect pressure comes from the situation and social cues.

stem: Match each response to passive, aggressive, or assertive communication.
options: ["Passive", "Aggressive", "Assertive"]
rows: ["Looks them in the eye and says, \"No thanks, I'm not interested.\"", "Mumbles \"um, maybe... okay\" and looks away", "Yells, \"You're stupid for asking!\"", "Says, \"Sure, whatever you want\" to avoid conflict"]
rationale: Assertive communication is clear and respectful; passive gives in and aggressive attacks.

stem: Which are effective refusal or exit strategies? Select all that apply.
options: ["Leaving the setting and contacting a trusted adult", "Going along now and planning to quit later", "Teaming up with a friend who will leave with you", "Giving a long, apologetic explanation hoping they stop asking", "Saying a clear \"No thanks\" and suggesting something else to do"]
rationale: Short, confident refusals, alternatives, allies, and leaving are effective; long excuses and going along are not.

stem: Which response uses effective body language and concise words?
options: ["Looking at the floor and saying, \"maybe, I guess\"", "Laughing nervously while giving a long, rambling excuse", "Standing close to the person and shouting a long insult", "Eye contact, a calm voice, and \"No thanks, I'm good.\""]
rationale: Confident posture and a brief, clear statement make refusal more effective.

stem: A fictional friend at a party is unresponsive after drinking. What is the best action?
options: ["Handle it alone so that no one else ever finds out", "Keep it secret to protect the friend from trouble", "Call for emergency help and get a trusted adult", "Wait until the morning to see how they are doing"]
rationale: Safety comes before secrecy; some situations need an adult or emergency help immediately.

stem: Match each description to the correct term.
options: ["Probability", "House edge", "Gambler's fallacy"]
rows: ["The built-in advantage that lets the business win over time", "The percentage of bets a game is designed to keep on average", "The math of how likely an event is to happen", "Believing a long losing streak means a win is \"due\""]
rationale: Probability measures chance, house edge is the game's built-in advantage, and the gambler's fallacy is a false belief about streaks.

stem: A fair coin lands on heads five times in a row. Which statement is true about the next flip?
options: ["The coin must be broken, so the next result is unpredictable.", "It still has a 50% chance of tails, since flips are independent.", "Heads is now certain to continue, since it is on a streak.", "Tails is now more likely, because the coin must balance out."]
rationale: Believing tails is "due" is the gambler's fallacy; past results do not change the odds of an independent event.

stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability of rolling a 4?
rationale: One of six equally likely outcomes is a 4, so the probability is 1/6.

stem: A game costs $2 to play. There is a 1-in-10 chance to win $10 and otherwise you win nothing. What is the expected result per play, on average?
options: ["Break even ($0)", "A loss of $1 per play", "A gain of about $8 per play on average", "A gain of $1 per play"]
rationale: Expected value is (1/10 x $10) - $2 = -$1, so players lose on average.

stem: Why does a gambling business profit over time even though some players win?
options: ["The business secretly decides who wins and who loses each time.", "Players who learn the right system eventually beat the odds.", "Games pay out less than the true odds, so the house wins.", "Winners always give their money back to the game the next day."]
rationale: House advantage guarantees an average profit for the business over many bets.

stem: Match each fictional example to the term it shows.
options: ["Variable reinforcement", "Near miss", "Chasing losses", "Tolerance"]
rows: ["A spin stops one symbol short of the jackpot", "Wins arrive at unpredictable times, like a slot machine", "Needing larger bets to feel the same excitement", "Betting bigger to win back money already lost"]
rationale: These are the key patterns that keep reward systems engaged and keep people gambling.

stem: Why do unpredictable rewards, like slot machine payouts, keep people playing?
options: ["Players always know exactly when the next win is coming.", "Predictable rewards cause the stronger and longer dopamine response.", "Dopamine is released only at the moment a player wins money.", "Unpredictable rewards trigger a stronger, longer dopamine response."]
rationale: Variable reinforcement produces a strong, persistent reward response.

stem: Which statement describes the mismatch in the teen brain?
options: ["Teen brains have no reward system, which explains the risk-taking.", "The prefrontal cortex finishes maturing before the reward system does.", "The reward system matures first, while impulse control in the prefrontal cortex lags.", "Both brain systems are already fully mature by about age twelve."]
rationale: Reward-seeking develops before impulse control and judgment finish maturing.

stem: Why does that mismatch raise teens' vulnerability to gambling and other addictive behaviors?
options: ["Teens are less able to understand the rules of games than adults are.", "Teens cannot feel rewards, so they keep looking for more.", "Strong reward-seeking and still-maturing impulse control make stopping harder.", "Teens always understand the odds, so they are fully protected."]
rationale: The gap between reward drive and self-control increases the risk of developing addictive patterns.

stem: Which can raise a person's vulnerability to problem gambling? Select all that apply.
options: ["Early exposure to gambling or gambling-like games", "Strong support from trusted adults", "Knowing the odds of a game", "High impulsivity", "Strong reward-seeking"]
rationale: Impulsivity, reward-seeking, and early exposure raise risk; support and understanding odds are protective.

stem: Match each fictional ad line to the technique it uses.
options: ["Sign-up bonus or \"risk-free\" bet", "Celebrity or influencer promotion", "Streak or loyalty reward", "Social proof"]
rows: ["\"You're on a 5-day streak. Bet again to unlock a bonus!\"", "\"Join millions of fans already betting!\"", "A famous player says he bets on every game he watches", "\"Your first bet is risk-free up to $100!\""]
rationale: Bonuses, famous faces, rewards for staying active, and crowd appeal are common betting marketing tactics.

stem: Which are persuasive techniques used in sports-betting ads? Select all that apply.
options: ["Explaining the house edge to viewers", "Sign-up bonuses", "Showing the true odds of losing in large print", "Loyalty or streak rewards", "\"Risk-free bet\" language", "Celebrity endorsements"]
rationale: Ads highlight excitement and rewards and rarely show the odds or the house edge.

stem: A fictional betting app promo uses game-style graphics, popular streamers, and meme slang. Which audience is it most likely aiming for?
options: ["Professional gamblers", "Teens and young adults", "Elementary-aged children", "Retired adults"]
rationale: Style, platforms, and language show who an ad wants to reach.

stem: How can constant betting ads during sports broadcasts normalize gambling for young people?
options: ["It makes betting seem rare and unusual among sports fans.", "It has no effect, because teens cannot legally place any bets.", "Betting paired with fandom and celebrities seems like a normal part of sports.", "It teaches viewers the real odds and risks behind every bet."]
rationale: Repeated exposure shapes what feels normal, even for people who cannot yet bet.

stem: Why is a "risk-free bet" not really risk-free?
options: ["The odds change in the player's favor during the promotion.", "The company covers every loss with no conditions attached at all.", "Bonuses come with conditions, so money must be wagered first.", "Risk-free bets are guaranteed to never lose any money at all."]
rationale: The wording hides the conditions and keeps the player betting.

stem: Which could be warning signs of problem gambling? Select all that apply.
options: ["Betting more to win back lost money", "Skipping school or activities to gamble", "Borrowing money repeatedly", "Lying about losses", "Spending time on hobbies and friends", "Choosing not to bet"]
rationale: Hiding behavior, money problems, chasing losses, and neglecting responsibilities are warning signs.

stem: Chris (fictional) is invited to join a betting pool. Match each statement to the decision-making step.
options: ["Identify the problem", "List options", "Think about consequences", "Make the decision"]
rows: ["Chris declines and suggests a pickup game", "Chris is asked to put money into a betting pool", "Losing money, feeling pressure again, straining friendships", "Join, say no, or suggest another activity"]
rationale: A decision-making model moves from the problem to options, consequences, and a choice.

stem: Which is the clearest refusal to a friend pressuring you to join a betting pool?
options: ["\"I'd join, but I would probably get caught by someone.\"", "\"Maybe next time, I guess, if I have some extra money.\"", "\"No thanks, I'm not in. Want to play basketball?\"", "\"That's a dumb thing to do and you should feel bad!\""]
rationale: A clear, calm "no" with an alternative is an effective refusal.

stem: Where can someone find help for problem gambling? Select all that apply.
options: ["Keep it secret and handle it alone", "A school counselor", "A trusted adult", "Borrow money from friends to cover losses", "The National Problem Gambling Helpline, 1-800-522-4700"]
rationale: Counselors, trusted adults, and the helpline offer support; secrecy and borrowing make things worse.

stem: Sort each consequence of problem gambling as financial or social.
options: ["Financial consequence", "Social consequence"]
rows: ["Missing team events or school to gamble", "Friends or family losing trust after lies about losses", "Losing money needed for everyday things", "Borrowing money and not repaying it"]
rationale: Problem gambling harms both money and relationships.

stem: A CDC data card reports that of 1,658 teens (ages 16-19) killed in car crashes in 2020 with known belt use, 936 were not wearing a seat belt. What is the main finding?
options: ["Most of the teens who were killed had been wearing seat belts.", "Seat belts caused more than half of these teen deaths.", "More than half of the teens killed were not buckled up.", "Only a small share of the teens killed were unbuckled."]
rationale: 936 of 1,658 is about 56%. Summarizing a data card means stating what the numbers show. (Figure from the CDC teen driver risk-factors page; swap in the latest CDC or NHTSA numbers when you teach.)

stem: Which source would give the most credible injury statistics?
options: ["An ad for a car accessory", "CDC WISQARS or NHTSA", "A meme with no source", "A friend's story"]
rationale: Credible statistics come from government health and safety agencies that publish their data.

stem: How does a seatbelt reduce the risk of serious injury in a crash?
options: ["It spreads crash force across the body and keeps you inside the vehicle.", "It only protects the driver, not the passengers in the car.", "It makes the car itself stop faster than it otherwise would.", "It prevents the crash from ever happening in the first place."]
rationale: Seatbelts reduce the force on the body and keep people inside the protective space of the vehicle.

stem: How does a helmet reduce the risk of serious head injury?
options: ["It cushions the impact so the head takes less force.", "It protects only the face and jaw, not the rest of the head.", "It prevents crashes and falls from happening in the first place.", "It only matters for beginners who are learning to ride."]
rationale: Helmets reduce the force that reaches the head and brain at any skill level.

stem: Sort each statement as a myth or a fact.
options: ["Myth", "Fact"]
rows: ["\"Wearing a helmet reduces the risk of serious head injury.\"", "\"Helmets are only necessary for beginners.\"", "\"Many serious teen injuries are predictable and preventable.\"", "\"I'm a good driver, so I don't need a seatbelt.\""]
rationale: Skill does not replace protective gear, and many injuries can be prevented with simple habits.

stem: A person suddenly collapses and is not breathing normally. What are the first two steps in the Chain of Survival?
options: ["Move them to a car, then drive to the hospital", "Give rescue breaths, then check a pulse for a minute", "Wait to see if they wake up, then call a parent", "Recognize the emergency and call 911"]
rationale: The first links are recognizing cardiac arrest and calling 911 right away.

stem: Which are links in the Chain of Survival? Select all that apply.
options: ["Hand off to EMS when they arrive", "Start compressions", "Recognize and call 911", "Give the person water", "Wait for symptoms to pass", "Use an AED"]
rationale: The chain is recognize, call 911, compress, use an AED, and hand off to EMS.

stem: Where do you place your hands for hands-only CPR on an adult?
options: ["On the left side of the chest, right over the heart", "On the center of the chest, hands stacked", "On the upper stomach, just below the ribs", "On the neck, with both hands pressing near the throat"]
rationale: Compressions go on the center of the chest.

stem: Which rhythm matches the recommended compression rate for hands-only CPR?
options: ["As fast as possible, about 180 compressions per minute", "Fast, then slow, then fast again in a repeating pattern", "A steady 100 to 120 compressions per minute", "A slow, careful pace of about 60 compressions per minute"]
rationale: A steady rate of 100 to 120 per minute keeps blood moving effectively.

stem: Which best describes hands-only CPR?
options: ["Giving rescue breaths only, with no chest compressions", "One minute of compressions, then stopping to wait for EMS", "Gentle chest presses once every few seconds until help comes", "Nonstop hard, fast chest compressions, no breaths"]
rationale: Hands-only CPR is recommended for teens and adults who see someone suddenly collapse.

stem: Put the AED steps in order. Match each step to when it happens.
options: ["First", "Second", "Third", "Fourth"]
rows: ["Turn on the AED and follow its voice prompts", "Make sure no one is touching the person while it analyzes or shocks", "Resume CPR when the AED says to", "Attach the pads to bare skin as pictured"]
rationale: The sequence is power on, pads on, stand clear, then resume CPR as prompted.

stem: The AED has delivered a shock. What should you do next?
options: ["Wait about ten minutes before touching the person again", "Resume CPR right away or when the AED prompts you", "Remove the pads and stop", "Wait for the person to sit up on their own"]
rationale: CPR continues after a shock until the AED prompts otherwise or EMS takes over.

stem: How do CPR and an AED work together in the Chain of Survival?
options: ["CPR keeps blood moving while an AED checks and shocks the heart if needed.", "An AED replaces the need for CPR once it has been turned on.", "Either one used alone is always enough to save a person.", "CPR is only started after the AED has already failed twice."]
rationale: CPR, the AED, and calling 911 together make up the response most likely to save a life.

stem: Myth: "Doctors will not try as hard to save a registered organ donor." Which fact corrects it?
options: ["Doctors only try hard to save donors who are very young.", "Registering is a legal contract that replaces normal medical care.", "Registered donors get the same life-saving care as anyone else.", "Registered donors are treated after other patients are seen."]
rationale: Being a registered donor does not change the medical care a person receives.

stem: Myth: "Organ donation rules out an open-casket funeral." Which fact corrects it?
options: ["Donors cannot have any service.", "Donation always rules out a funeral.", "Donation does not prevent an open-casket funeral.", "Only some religions allow funerals after donation."]
rationale: Donation is performed with care and does not stop families from having a viewing or service.

stem: In a ruler-drop test, students catch the ruler more slowly while also reading a text aloud. What does this show?
options: ["Only physical distractions, like holding a phone, slow reactions.", "Reaction time stays the same no matter how much attention is split.", "Distraction slows reaction time, so a driver travels farther before reacting.", "Multitasking sharpens reaction time by keeping the brain busy."]
rationale: Divided attention measurably delays response, which raises crash risk.

stem: Match each example to the type of distraction it shows.
options: ["Visual", "Manual", "Cognitive"]
rows: ["Looking away from the road at a notification", "Reading a text while crossing a street", "Mind busy replaying an argument", "Taking a hand off the wheel to type"]
rationale: Distractions can take eyes, hands, or attention away from the task.

stem: Why is texting while driving especially dangerous?
options: ["It only distracts the eyes and not the hands or the mind.", "It is safe at low speeds, so it matters little in town.", "It combines visual, manual, and cognitive distraction.", "It only matters on highways and never on side streets."]
rationale: Texting takes the eyes, hands, and mind off driving at once.

stem: Which are healthy technology habits that support safety? Select all that apply.
options: ["Being careful about sharing real-time location publicly", "Sharing your live location publicly so friends can find you", "Setting boundaries around notifications", "Not using a phone while crossing streets", "Using do-not-disturb driving mode or keeping the phone out of reach", "Texting only at red lights while driving"]
rationale: Safe habits limit distractions and protect privacy; public live location and texting at lights add risk.

stem: Which is a specific, realistic safety commitment for a fictional student?
options: ["\"I will try to be a lot safer when I am driving.\"", "\"I will never use any kind of technology ever again.\"", "\"I will put my phone in my bag before I drive.\"", "\"I will only text when I feel like it is safe to.\""]
rationale: A strong commitment names a specific action, a time, and is realistic to follow.

stem: Match each job to the macronutrient that does it.
options: ["Carbohydrates", "Protein", "Fat"]
rows: ["Builds and repairs body tissue", "Stores energy and supports cell function", "Found mostly in foods like bread, rice, and fruit", "The body's main source of energy"]
rationale: Carbohydrates fuel the body, protein builds and repairs, and fat stores energy and supports cells.

stem: Which foods are mostly protein? Select all that apply.
options: ["Eggs", "White rice", "Olive oil", "Grilled chicken", "Tofu"]
rationale: Chicken, tofu, and eggs are protein-rich; rice is mostly carbohydrate and olive oil is mostly fat.

stem: Which fictional lunch best matches the MyPlate proportions?
options: ["A large order of fries, onion rings, and a big soda", "Two slices of pizza, a bag of chips, and a sugary drink", "Grilled chicken, brown rice, broccoli, an apple, and milk", "A large bowl of fruit salad with nothing else on the plate"]
rationale: A MyPlate meal includes fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, and dairy in balanced proportions.

stem: How is MyPlate best described?
options: ["A list of foods that people should never eat", "A strict plan that every meal must match exactly", "A weight-loss diet that restricts certain foods", "A guide showing balance, not a strict rule"]
rationale: MyPlate shows balance across food groups rather than one perfect meal.

stem: What do micronutrients do?
options: ["They are simply another name for the fats in food.", "Vitamins and minerals help the body in small amounts.", "They provide most of the body's daily energy supply.", "They can only be obtained by taking a supplement pill."]
rationale: Micronutrients are needed in small amounts and are found in a variety of foods.

stem: Match each description to the part of the nutrition facts label.
options: ["Serving size", "Calories", "% Daily Value", "Added sugars"]
rows: ["The standard amount that all the numbers on the label are based on", "Sugars put in during processing, not found naturally", "The energy you get from one serving", "A rough guide to how much a serving adds toward a day's needs"]
rationale: Each part of the label answers a different question about the food.

stem: A nutrient lists 25% Daily Value per serving. How is that generally described?
options: ["Not important", "Exactly right for one meal", "Low (5% or less)", "High (20% or more)"]
rationale: A rough guide: 5% or less is low and 20% or more is high.

stem: Cereal A has 12 g added sugar per serving and Cereal B has 5 g per serving, with the same serving size. Which statement is accurate?
options: ["The label cannot be used to compare two different cereals.", "Cereal A has less added sugar.", "They have the same added sugar.", "Cereal B has less added sugar per serving."]
rationale: Comparing the same serving size on both labels shows which has less added sugar.

stem: A bag lists 2 servings with 150 calories each. A student eats the whole bag. How many calories did they eat, and what does the serving size on the label mean?
options: ["300 calories; serving size is the amount everyone should eat.", "75 calories; labels list only half of a serving each time.", "300 calories; serving size is only a reference amount.", "150 calories; the label always shows the whole bag's total."]
rationale: Portion size is what a person actually eats; serving size is just a standard amount for comparison.

stem: Match each visual reference to what it can help estimate.
options: ["Palm", "Fist", "Cupped hand", "Thumb"]
rows: ["About one serving of meat or other protein", "About a serving of peanut butter or oil", "About a small handful-sized snack portion", "About a cup of cooked pasta or fruit"]
rationale: Hand-based references are a practical estimating tool, not a strict rule.

stem: Match each description to the FITT component.
options: ["Frequency", "Intensity", "Time", "Type"]
rows: ["How many minutes each session lasts", "How hard the body is working", "Walking, swimming, or strength training", "How many days per week"]
rationale: FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time, and Type.

stem: Kai (fictional) walks at an easy pace for 20 minutes on 2 days a week. Which change increases the Frequency component?
options: ["Swimming instead of walking", "Adding short jogging intervals", "Walking for 30 minutes each time instead of 20", "Walking on 4 days a week instead of 2"]
rationale: Frequency is how often; the other choices change time, intensity, and type.

stem: Which activity plan includes all four FITT components?
options: ["Jog for 30 minutes on 3 days a week at no particular effort level", "Jog at a moderate pace for 30 minutes on 3 days a week", "Jog at a moderate pace for 30 minutes whenever there is time", "Jog at a moderate pace on 3 days a week as time allows"]
rationale: A FITT plan names how often, how hard, how long, and what kind of activity.

stem: During an activity a student can say only a few words at a time. Using the talk test, what is the intensity?
options: ["Light, because they can still talk easily", "Moderate, because they can sing easily", "It cannot be judged using the talk test", "Vigorous, because talking is difficult"]
rationale: If you can only say a few words, the activity is vigorous.

stem: A student rates their effort 3 out of 10 and can sing easily. What does this suggest about intensity?
options: ["Vigorous, because the effort rating is high", "Moderate, because singing is easy", "It cannot be judged from an effort rating", "Light, because the effort rating is low"]
rationale: A low effort rating and easy singing show light intensity.

stem: Match each example to the marketing technique it uses.
options: ["Health halo (front-label claim)", "Influencer promotion", "Dramatic before/after claim"]
rows: ["Photos showing a huge change in two weeks", "\"100% NATURAL! LOW FAT!\" on a package that is high in added sugar", "\"Natural\" printed in large type on a candy wrapper", "A fitness creator holding a supplement with a discount code"]
rationale: Front-label claims, influencer promotion, and dramatic before/after images are common patterns.

stem: A snack bar front says "Made with real fruit!" but the label shows 18 g of added sugar. Which technique is this?
options: ["A health halo: a front claim hides the real label.", "A medical recommendation from a doctor or a dietitian", "Social proof, because many other buyers like the product", "A scarcity claim, because the bar seems to be a limited item"]
rationale: The front claim draws attention while the added sugar is on the full label.

stem: Which are common patterns in social-media fitness marketing? Select all that apply.
options: ["Influencer-promoted supplements", "Linked studies from credible organizations", "Claims of fast or extreme results", "Dramatic before/after images", "Balanced advice from a registered dietitian"]
rationale: These patterns grab attention without giving reliable evidence.

stem: Why should a fitness claim be checked against a credible source?
options: ["Front-of-package claims must always give the complete picture.", "If many people follow a claim, it has already been verified.", "Marketing grabs attention, while credible sources show the evidence.", "Influencers are always trained experts in nutrition and fitness."]
rationale: Credible sources, like a registered dietitian or public health organization, provide the real picture.

stem: Which are credible sources for checking a fitness or nutrition claim? Select all that apply.
options: ["An established public health organization", "A doctor", "An influencer's discount-code page", "A registered dietitian", "An anonymous comment"]
rationale: Experts and public health organizations are credible; sellers and anonymous posts are not.

stem: Which goal includes all five SMART components?
options: ["I will eat vegetables at every single meal for the rest of my whole life.", "I will add one serving of vegetables to dinner on four nights each week.", "I will add a serving of vegetables to dinner 4 nights a week for 4 weeks to get more fiber.", "I will eat more vegetables at dinner and try to be healthier overall soon."]
rationale: The goal names an action, a number, a realistic target, a reason, and a time frame.

stem: Match each phrase from a goal to the SMART component it shows.
options: ["Specific", "Measurable", "Achievable", "Relevant", "Time-bound"]
rows: ["\"for the next three weeks\"", "\"on 4 days a week\"", "\"to keep my energy up for practice\"", "\"using fruit I already have at home\"", "\"add a serving of fruit to breakfast\""]
rationale: Each part of a SMART goal answers a different question.

stem: Which is a habit-based nutrition or activity goal?
options: ["Change my body shape to look like someone online.", "Stay under a set number of calories every single day.", "Add one serving of vegetables to dinner four nights this week.", "Lose 10 pounds by the end of June, whatever it takes."]
rationale: Habit-based goals focus on actions, not weight, calories, or body size.

stem: Which are realistic barriers to a goal of eating breakfast before school? Select all that apply.
options: ["Not feeling hungry early in the day", "Not enough time in the morning", "Writing the goal down", "No grab-and-go options at home", "Having a clear goal"]
rationale: A barrier is something that could get in the way of the goal.

stem: Barrier: "I don't have time before school." Which strategy fits?
options: ["Skip breakfast entirely on those mornings", "Wait until there is more free time in the mornings", "Prepare something the night before", "Drop the goal because it is too hard to keep"]
rationale: A strategy directly addresses the barrier.

stem: Sort each statement about puberty as a myth or a fact.
options: ["Myth", "Fact"]
rows: ["Puberty includes both physical and emotional changes.", "The timing and pace of puberty vary widely and are normal.", "Everyone goes through puberty at exactly the same age.", "If puberty starts later than friends', something is wrong."]
rationale: Puberty timing varies, and changes are physical, emotional, and social.

stem: Several of Maya's (fictional) friends started puberty earlier than she did. Which statement is most accurate?
options: ["Her body will probably skip puberty altogether.", "Everyone should start puberty at exactly the same age.", "She must have a health problem that needs treatment.", "Timing varies from person to person and is normal."]
rationale: There is a wide, normal range for when puberty begins.

stem: Which changes can happen during puberty? Select all that apply.
options: ["Height and weight stay exactly the same", "Growth spurts", "The brain stops developing", "Changes in social interests", "Hormonal changes", "Mood and emotional changes"]
rationale: Puberty involves physical, hormonal, emotional, and social changes.

stem: Which is the most reliable place to get an answer about puberty or body changes?
options: ["A doctor, the school nurse, or KidsHealth", "An anonymous post in a public online forum", "An ad for a product that claims to fix it", "A rumor that gets passed along in the hallway"]
rationale: Reliable information comes from health professionals and recognized health organizations.

stem: Which are signs of a reliable health website? Select all that apply.
options: ["It is run by a recognized health organization", "It has no author or sources", "It is mainly trying to sell a product", "It cites medical sources"]
rationale: Credible sources are run by experts, cite evidence, and are not mainly selling something.

stem: Sort each characteristic as healthy or unhealthy in a relationship.
options: ["Healthy", "Unhealthy"]
rows: ["Pressuring someone to do things they do not want to do", "Controlling who the other person can talk to", "Honesty and trust", "Respect for each other's opinions"]
rationale: Healthy relationships have respect, trust, and equality; control and pressure are unhealthy.

stem: Which are warning signs of an unhealthy relationship? Select all that apply.
options: ["Pressure", "Spending time with other friends", "Isolation from friends and family", "Disrespect", "Control over decisions", "Disagreeing and talking it through respectfully"]
rationale: Isolation, control, pressure, and disrespect are warning signs; respectful disagreement is normal.

stem: Which statement correctly describes consent?
options: ["Once given, it can never be changed or taken back.", "Silence from the other person always means yes.", "Asking over and over until someone agrees is fine.", "It is clear, freely given, and can be withdrawn at any time."]
rationale: Consent must be freely given and can be taken back at any time.

stem: What is a personal boundary?
options: ["A limit set for what someone is comfortable with", "Something that only counts if the other person agrees", "A way to punish someone who has upset you in the past", "A rule that applies only in romantic relationships"]
rationale: Boundaries apply in every relationship, including friendships and family.

stem: A group-project partner keeps ignoring a student's ideas. Which statement sets a boundary clearly and respectfully?
options: ["\"I feel ignored when my ideas get skipped. Please listen.\"", "\"Fine, whatever, just do it your way and leave me out.\"", "\"You never listen to anyone and you are completely useless.\"", "\"I will just do the whole project all by myself.\""]
rationale: A clear, respectful boundary names the feeling, the situation, and what is needed.

stem: Sort each way as one that can or cannot spread HIV.
options: ["Can spread HIV", "Cannot spread HIV"]
rows: ["From a parent to a baby during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding", "Sharing needles", "Mosquito bites", "Hugging"]
rationale: HIV spreads only through certain body fluids; it does not spread through casual contact or insects.

stem: Which statement about STIs is accurate?
options: ["All STIs can be cured with a short course of antibiotics.", "Only certain kinds of people can ever get an STI.", "STIs always cause symptoms that a person can easily see.", "Some are curable, some are manageable, and many show no symptoms."]
rationale: Many STIs have no symptoms, which is why testing matters for anyone who is sexually active.

stem: Which are prevention methods for STIs? Select all that apply.
options: ["Abstinence", "Vaccination where available, such as the HPV vaccine", "Correct and consistent condom use (reduces, but does not eliminate, risk)", "Birth control pills (they prevent pregnancy, not STIs)", "Washing up after contact", "Regular testing"]
rationale: Abstinence, vaccination, testing, and condoms help; birth control pills do not protect against STIs.

stem: Which prevention method has no risk of sexually transmitted infection?
options: ["Abstinence, which removes the risk entirely", "Regular testing, which finds infections early", "Correct and consistent condom use, which lowers risk", "Vaccination, which protects against some infections"]
rationale: Other methods reduce risk, but abstinence removes it entirely.

stem: Sort each HIV statement as a myth or a fact.
options: ["Myth", "Fact"]
rows: ["HIV can spread by sharing food or drinks.", "HIV can spread through hugging.", "Stigma and misinformation harm people living with HIV.", "With modern treatment, HIV is a manageable long-term condition."]
rationale: Accurate information reduces stigma and fear.

stem: Why is abstinence presented as the most effective prevention method?
options: ["Because it is the easiest choice for every single person to make.", "Because no other prevention method has any effect on either one.", "Because it only matters for one particular group of people.", "Because it removes the risk of pregnancy and STIs, while others only reduce it."]
rationale: Abstinence is the only method with no risk; others reduce risk but do not eliminate it.

stem: Which statement about choosing abstinence is accurate?
options: ["It can be chosen and re-affirmed at any point, for many reasons.", "It cannot be changed once a person has decided on it.", "It is only ever chosen for one particular reason.", "It only counts if a person has never faced any pressure."]
rationale: People choose abstinence for values, goals, readiness, or health reasons, and can re-affirm the decision at any time.

stem: A fictional teen feels pressured. Match each statement to the decision-making step.
options: ["Identify the situation and values", "List options", "Weigh consequences", "Decide", "Reflect"]
rows: ["Pressure may continue, but saying no protects my values and health", "A partner is pressuring me, and I want to wait", "Later, I think about what worked and what I would do differently", "I will say no and suggest something else to do", "I can say no, change the subject, leave, or talk to a trusted adult"]
rationale: A decision-making model moves from the situation and values to options, consequences, a decision, and reflection.

stem: Which is a clear, respectful refusal that stays consistent with personal values?
options: ["\"No, I'm not ready, and that's okay. Let's go.\"", "\"I guess so, if you really want to, I suppose.\"", "\"Maybe later, I guess, I don't really know yet...\"", "\"You're pathetic for even asking me something like that.\""]
rationale: Clear, calm, and respectful language protects boundaries and the relationship.

stem: Which strategies help someone stay consistent with their values under pressure? Select all that apply.
options: ["Talking with a trusted adult", "Giving a long explanation hoping the pressure stops", "Leaving the situation", "Planning a response ahead of time", "Going along to avoid conflict"]
rationale: Planning, exit strategies, and support work better than going along or over-explaining.

stem: Which are reliable resources for health information? Select all that apply.
options: ["A trusted doctor", "An anonymous forum", "The CDC", "An ad with miracle-cure claims", "The local health department", "The school nurse or counselor"]
rationale: Health professionals and recognized health organizations are reliable.

stem: A fictional friend is worried about a health question and does not know who to ask. Which two resources would you name?
options: ["No one at all; they should simply handle it alone", "An anonymous online forum and an ad for a product", "A rumor in a group chat and a popular influencer", "The school nurse and a trusted doctor"]
rationale: Reliable, accessible resources include the school nurse or counselor and a trusted doctor.

stem: What is generally true about testing and health services for minors?
options: ["They are always completely free and fully confidential everywhere.", "Only a parent is allowed to find out where to go for help.", "Rules vary by state and provider, so ask a school nurse or counselor first.", "They are never available to any person who is under eighteen."]
