rationale: Rules differ by state and provider; a nurse or counselor can explain what is available locally.

stem: Which are good first places to ask where to get testing or help? Select all that apply.
options: ["Rumors in a group chat", "The school counselor", "A trusted doctor", "A social media influencer", "The school nurse", "The local health department"]
rationale: Professionals and public-health offices can give accurate local information.

stem: Which message to a friend is accurate and non-judgmental?
options: ["\"Everyone will find out about it, so you had better be careful.\"", "\"I care about you. The school nurse can help, and asking is okay.\"", "\"Just google it yourself, because honestly I do not care.\"", "\"You should be ashamed to even need help with something like this.\""]
rationale: An effective message is caring, accurate, and free of shame.

stem: Which of these would a school nurse or doctor record as health metrics? Select all that apply.
options: ["Body temperature", "Weight", "Number of video game wins", "Pulse rate (heart rate)", "Favorite sport to watch"]
rationale: Temperature, weight, and pulse are measurable facts about the body that clinics track.

stem: Sort each fictional person's result as a positive health metric or one that needs attention.
options: ["Positive metric", "Needs attention"]
rows: ["Sleeping only about 4 hours on most school nights", "Up-to-date vaccinations", "Body temperature of 98.6 degrees F at a routine checkup", "Resting heart rate far above the normal range at several visits"]
rationale: Metrics inside healthy ranges are positive; repeated readings outside them are a signal to follow up.

stem: Priya's resting heart rate was a little high at one clinic visit. Which statement about health metrics is the most accurate?
options: ["Any number outside the usual range means the person has a disease.", "The healthy range is the same for toddlers, teens, and older adults.", "One reading gives a complete and final picture of a person's health.", "A single reading is a snapshot, and patterns over time matter."]
rationale: Metrics are best interpreted over time and with a health professional.

stem: Sort each lifestyle factor by whether it generally supports health or diminishes it.
options: ["Supports health", "Diminishes health"]
rows: ["Drinking water throughout the day", "Spending free time being active outdoors", "Smoking or vaping regularly", "Skipping meals and relying on sugary drinks"]
rationale: Hydration and activity support health; tobacco, nicotine, and poor eating habits harm it.

stem: Leo (fictional) sleeps 5 hours, eats few vegetables, and rarely moves during the day. Which plan would most likely improve his health metrics?
options: ["Use energy drinks to stay awake and skip meals to save time.", "Add daily movement, eat vegetables, and aim for more sleep.", "Do one very hard workout a month to make up for everything else.", "Ignore his health numbers since they are only numbers."]
rationale: Small, steady changes in movement, eating, and sleep improve many metrics together.

stem: Which of these are physical health metrics? Select all that apply.
options: ["How well a person copes with stress", "Height and weight", "Amount of weekly exercise", "How many people a person trusts", "Blood pressure"]
rationale: Physical metrics measure the body and its habits.

stem: Which is the best example of a mental health metric?
options: ["How many minutes of exercise a person gets daily", "How well a person can focus and manage worries", "A person's height and weight at a checkup", "How many people a person talks to each day"]
rationale: Mental health metrics describe focus, stress, and coping.

stem: A fictional student skips meals and sleeps 4 hours, and then feels anxious and cannot concentrate. What does this show about wellness?
options: ["Only mental wellness matters when a student is struggling.", "Physical habits have no connection to how a person feels.", "Physical habits and mental wellness are linked.", "Anxiety is only caused by schoolwork, never by daily habits."]
rationale: Sleep and nutrition influence mood and focus, so the dimensions of wellness are connected.

stem: Omar (fictional) feels overwhelmed and snaps at others when he is frustrated, even though he has good friends. Which dimension is mostly affected?
options: ["Financial wellness", "Emotional wellness", "Environmental wellness", "Physical wellness"]
rationale: Understanding and managing feelings is an emotional wellness skill.

stem: Sort each example by the dimension it best shows.
options: ["Social wellness", "Emotional wellness"]
rows: ["Resolves conflicts by talking respectfully", "Spends time with supportive friends and family", "Notices feeling sad and uses a healthy way to cope", "Handles a bad grade without losing control"]
rationale: Social wellness is about connections; emotional wellness is about understanding and managing feelings.

stem: Which is the best description of a wellness self-assessment?
options: ["A reflection tool for noticing habits, strengths, and areas to grow", "A one-time test that decides whether someone is healthy", "A medical exam that diagnoses health problems", "A graded quiz used to rank students against each other"]
rationale: A self-assessment is for honest reflection, not ranking or diagnosing.

stem: Sam's (fictional) self-assessment shows stress management 2 out of 5, sleep 4 out of 5, and social connection 3 out of 5. What are his strength and his area to improve?
options: ["He has no strengths since none of his scores is a 5.", "Strength: social connection. Area to improve: sleep and stress.", "Strength: sleep. Area to improve: stress management.", "Strength: stress management. Area to improve: sleep."]
rationale: His highest score is a strength and his lowest score is the clearest area to improve.

stem: Match each description to the SMART letter it shows.
options: ["Specific", "Measurable", "Achievable", "Relevant", "Time-bound"]
rows: ["Tracks progress by counting 5 mornings a week", "Will be done daily until the end of the semester", "Fits into the existing school-day schedule", "Plans to stretch for 10 minutes each morning", "Helps relieve tightness from sitting all day"]
rationale: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.

stem: A goal says, "Eat better." Which revision fixes the missing SMART parts?
options: ["Eat only fruit and vegetables for the next two full months.", "Eat healthier foods more often and avoid junk food from now on.", "Eat one fruit with lunch on 5 school days a week for 4 weeks.", "Never eat any snacks or desserts again, starting from today."]
rationale: The revision names the action, a number, a realistic plan, and a time frame.

stem: Which of these goals include all five SMART parts? Select all that apply.
options: ["Do a 10-minute breathing exercise every evening for two weeks to reduce stress.", "Get in shape somehow.", "Feel happier.", "Walk to school on 3 mornings a week for the next month to build energy."]
rationale: A SMART goal names an action, a measure, a realistic target, a reason, and a deadline.

stem: Which are warning signs that a health claim may be misleading? Select all that apply.
options: ["Was reviewed by independent health experts", "Names the study and links to the full report", "Is selling the very product it recommends", "Says a product will \"melt fat\" with no effort", "Relies on a single photo of one person as proof"]
rationale: Effortless miracle results, thin proof, and a sales motive are common red flags.

stem: Sort each feature by whether it points to a credible source or a source to question.
options: ["Credible source", "Question this source"]
rows: ["Written by a doctor and cites published research", "A video saying \"doctors hate this one trick\"", "A state health department website", "A celebrity paid to promote a diet tea"]
rationale: Credible sources have expertise and evidence; paid promotion and clickbait do not.

stem: A famous YouTuber with millions of subscribers says a juice cleanse "resets your body." What does their fame show?
options: ["That the claim is true, because millions of people watch them.", "That the cleanse is safe because many viewers shared the video.", "Nothing about its truth, since credible evidence counts.", "That the claim is proven by how healthy the YouTuber looks."]
rationale: Fame, looks, and shares are not evidence; credibility comes from expertise and proof.

stem: What is the best way to check a surprising health claim you saw in a video?
options: ["Check how many likes and shares the video has received so far.", "Look for it from credible sources such as the CDC.", "Trust it when the speaker sounds confident and uses scientific words.", "Ask the commenters under the video whether the claim is true."]
rationale: Verification means comparing the claim with reliable, independent sources.

stem: A fictional post says a "detox" tea cleans your organs in three days. Which decision and reason are best?
options: ["Trust it: lots of followers commented that it worked for them.", "Trust it: natural ingredients are always safe and effective for everyone.", "Do not trust it yet: no evidence is shown, and the poster sells the tea.", "Do not trust it: anything sold online is always a scam."]
rationale: A good justification points to missing evidence and the seller's motive.

stem: Ava (fictional) has a big presentation tomorrow. At 10:30 p.m. friends invite her to a video chat. What decision does Ava face?
options: ["Which friend she should talk to first tonight", "Whether to give the presentation at all", "Whether to join the chat or go to bed", "Whether her friends are really her friends or not"]
rationale: The decision is the choice Ava must make now, and it affects her rest and her presentation.

stem: Mateo is tired, has homework left, and friends want to chat online. Which are realistic choices he could make? Select all that apply.
options: ["Do nothing and hope it all works out", "Tell friends he can chat tomorrow after school", "Stay up all night trying to do everything", "Finish homework, then go to bed on time", "Join the chat briefly, then stop at a set time"]
rationale: Realistic options fit his responsibilities; ignoring the situation solves nothing.

stem: Sort each consequence of regularly skipping breakfast.
options: ["Positive consequence", "Negative consequence"]
rows: ["Feeling hungry and distracted in morning classes", "Not having to prepare food in the morning", "A few extra minutes of sleep before school", "Low energy and trouble concentrating over time"]
rationale: Choices often have short-term upsides and longer-term costs; both belong in the decision.

stem: Which choice is the most responsible for a student who feels stressed and has stopped exercising and sleeping enough?
options: ["Set a realistic routine for sleep and movement and ask for help if needed.", "Keep pushing through and ignore how tired they feel.", "Copy what a friend does without thinking about the results.", "Stop doing schoolwork until the stress goes away on its own."]
rationale: A responsible choice considers consequences and supports health.

stem: Which statement best explains why a choice is a responsible health decision?
options: ["It is whatever choice is the most popular among classmates.", "It is the choice that an adult or authority figure picked for me.", "It considers short- and long-term effects and accepts ownership of the results.", "It is the choice that works out perfectly with no downside at all."]
rationale: Responsible decisions are based on consequences and ownership, not approval or perfection.

stem: Which statement best describes mental health?
options: ["Being in a good mood every moment of the day", "Whether a person has ever been diagnosed with a disorder", "How a person thinks, feels, and connects with others in daily life", "A term that applies only to people who need treatment"]
rationale: Everyone has mental health; it covers thoughts, feelings, and relationships.

stem: Which statement best explains why mental health is a continuum?
options: ["A person is either healthy or ill, and nothing moves them between.", "Only a doctor's diagnosis can place someone on the range.", "It stays fixed once a person becomes an adult.", "It ranges from thriving to struggling and can change."]
rationale: A continuum shows that mental health shifts with support, stress, and life events.

stem: Which statements are true about what can influence teen mental health? Select all that apply.
options: ["Online experiences, positive or negative, can affect it", "A heavy workload with little downtime can strain it", "Regular exercise and rest can support it", "Only a person's attitude matters; their surroundings do not", "Nothing can change it once a person turns thirteen", "Feeling accepted by classmates can protect it"]
rationale: Workload, belonging, habits, and online life all influence mental health.

stem: Sort each factor for a fictional teen as a risk factor or a protective factor.
options: ["Risk factor", "Protective factor"]
rows: ["A caring teacher or coach", "Being left out by classmates every day", "Constant conflict at home", "A routine with enough sleep and downtime"]
rationale: Risk factors raise the chance of struggling; protective factors help buffer stress.

stem: Which of these statements are inaccurate? Select all that apply.
options: ["Asking a counselor for help means a person is weak.", "People with mental illness can live full, productive lives.", "A person with a mental illness always looks sad or upset.", "A person's mental health can improve with support and time.", "Stress is always bad for you."]
rationale: These myths add stigma; mental health can improve and many people with illness thrive with support.

stem: Which fictional student's situation most likely suggests that extra support is needed?
options: ["Feels jittery before a school performance next week", "Feels exhausted after a week of final exams", "Stopped seeing friends and felt hopeless for a month", "Feels upset for an evening after a disagreement with a friend"]
rationale: Feelings that last for weeks and affect daily life go beyond an everyday challenge.

stem: Which could be warning signs that a person needs help? Select all that apply.
options: ["Needing time alone to recharge after a busy day", "Talking about feeling worthless or hopeless", "Losing interest in activities once enjoyed", "Grades dropping sharply with no clear reason", "Feeling excited before a big event", "Ongoing changes in sleep or eating"]
rationale: Lasting changes in mood, habits, and functioning are warning signs.

stem: Which part of the Duration, Intensity, Interference check does each detail show?
options: ["Duration", "Intensity", "Interference"]
rows: ["Worry feels so overwhelming it brings on panic", "These feelings have lasted since the fall", "Has stopped going to class and quit the team", "Has felt down nearly every day for two months"]
rationale: How long, how strong, and how much it disrupts life all help decide the level of concern.

stem: A fictional student shows several warning signs. Who is the most appropriate person to turn to first?
options: ["A video from a wellness influencer", "A school counselor or another trusted adult", "A stranger offering advice in a chat room", "Nobody, since signs usually pass without help"]
rationale: Counselors and trusted adults can assess the situation and connect the student to help.

stem: Why should a student refer a friend for help instead of diagnosing the friend?
options: ["Diagnosing a friend is the fastest way to solve the problem.", "Diagnosis takes professional training, so a peer can notice and refer.", "Peers can diagnose accurately by comparing symptoms to an online list.", "Warning signs are not important unless a doctor says so."]
rationale: Peers recognize and refer; diagnosing is for trained professionals.

stem: Which best describes what happens in the body during the stress response?
options: ["Heart rate drops so that energy is saved for later.", "Stress changes only thoughts and never affects the body.", "The body slows down so it can rest until the stress ends.", "The body speeds up heart rate and breathing to react."]
rationale: The stress response activates the body; recovery afterward matters.

stem: Sort each coping behavior as generally helpful or potentially harmful.
options: ["Generally helpful", "Potentially harmful"]
rows: ["Putting off every responsibility until the stress disappears", "Lashing out at other people when stressed", "Asking a friend or counselor for support", "Going for a walk to clear your head"]
rationale: Helpful coping manages stress or supports recovery; harmful coping avoids it or hurts others.

stem: Which are evidence-informed coping strategies? Select all that apply.
options: ["Ignoring the problem and hoping it disappears", "Short bursts of movement such as stretching", "Journaling to sort through worries", "Pushing through without sleep for days", "Taking slow breaths when feeling tense", "Planning tasks and tackling them one at a time"]
rationale: Journaling, movement, planning, and breathing help; skipping sleep and avoiding problems do not.

stem: Zoe (fictional) argued with a close friend and feels upset. Which strategy fits best?
options: ["Staying up all night replaying the argument", "Talking with a trusted person, then calmly reaching out", "Avoiding the friend forever and acting like nothing happened", "Posting angry messages about the friend online"]
rationale: Social stressors fit social support and calm communication.

stem: Which coping plan for a fictional student is the most realistic and complete?
options: ["Promises to never feel stressed again by working harder", "Names triggers, strategies, supporters, and when to seek help", "Relies on one favorite strategy even when it clearly stops working", "Keeps the plan secret and never asks anyone for help"]
rationale: A realistic plan matches strategies to stressors and includes support and a threshold for more help.

stem: Which show active listening? Select all that apply.
options: ["Changing the subject to something more cheerful", "Summarizing what you heard and checking that you got it right", "Making eye contact and facing the person", "Nodding and not interrupting while they talk", "Checking your phone while they talk"]
rationale: Active listening means full attention, patience, and checking understanding.

stem: Sort each response to a struggling friend as supportive or dismissive.
options: ["Supportive", "Dismissive"]
rows: ["Just cheer up, it could be worse.", "Thanks for trusting me with this.", "You're making a big deal out of nothing.", "That sounds like a lot to deal with."]
rationale: Supportive language validates feelings; dismissive language minimizes them.

stem: After listening to a friend who feels overwhelmed, which response best connects them to support?
options: ["\"Ask the internet and follow whatever it tells you to do.\"", "\"Would you like to see a counselor? I can come with you.\"", "\"Let's just ignore it for now and see if it goes away.\"", "\"Keep it to yourself, because it will probably pass soon.\""]
rationale: Offering to go with a friend to a trusted adult is a supportive, safe step.

stem: A friend asks you to keep a secret. In which situations must you involve a trusted adult? Select all that apply.
options: ["A friend says they want to hurt themselves", "A friend tells you someone is hurting them", "A friend is annoyed about a group chat argument", "A friend is nervous about a class presentation", "A friend says they plan to hurt another person"]
rationale: Safety comes before secrecy when someone may be hurt.

stem: A friend leans on you every day with serious problems. Which statement is accurate?
options: ["A good supporter must keep every secret regardless of safety.", "If the friend stays upset, the supporter failed.", "A good friend takes over as the friend's counselor.", "A good supporter listens and connects the friend to help."]
rationale: Friends are support, not treatment; trained helpers provide treatment.

stem: Which are sources of mental-health support for teens? Select all that apply.
options: ["A school psychologist or social worker", "A parent, caregiver, or coach they trust", "A comment section full of strangers", "A product page promising instant happiness", "A crisis text or phone line such as 988", "A therapist or counselor in the community"]
rationale: School staff, community professionals, trusted adults, and crisis lines are reliable supports.

stem: Sort each resource as crisis support or non-crisis support.
options: ["Crisis support", "Non-crisis support"]
rows: ["Texting or calling 988 during a crisis", "Asking the school nurse about local clinics", "Going to an emergency room when someone is in immediate danger", "Meeting a counselor weekly to build coping skills"]
rationale: Crisis resources are for immediate danger; non-crisis resources support ongoing needs.

stem: Which source is most likely to provide credible mental-health information?
options: ["A video by a person who is promoting a paid online course", "A medical center or government health site such as NIMH", "A viral post from someone who has no medical credentials", "A website with ads that promise instant, guaranteed results"]
rationale: Credible information comes from experts and evidence-based organizations.

stem: Ben (fictional) has felt anxious for weeks, but he is safe and not in danger. Which resource fits best?
options: ["Advice from unknown people on a message board", "A school counselor or health provider for support", "Waiting for the feelings to grow into a crisis first", "Calling 911 even though no emergency is happening"]
rationale: Ongoing, non-emergency concerns match counselors and health providers.

stem: Sort each strategy by the barrier to getting help it helps overcome.
options: ["Stigma or embarrassment", "Cost or transportation", "Not knowing where to go"]
rows: ["Use the school's resource list to see who to contact first", "Ask a trusted adult to help with rides", "Ask about free or sliding-scale services at the school or clinic", "Remember that many teens seek help and it takes courage"]
rationale: Naming the barrier makes it easier to pick a strategy that works.

stem: Which of these can influence the health of a community? Select all that apply.
options: ["Only the willpower of each resident", "Nothing outside a person's own body", "Safe neighborhoods and parks", "Housing conditions", "Clean drinking water", "Transportation to clinics and stores"]
rationale: Housing, transportation, safe spaces, and water quality all shape community health.

stem: Sort each example as an individual health behavior or an environmental influence.
options: ["Individual behavior", "Environmental influence"]
rows: ["Whether the nearest clinic can be reached by bus", "Choosing what to drink with dinner", "Whether the neighborhood has working streetlights and sidewalks", "Choosing to take the stairs"]
rationale: Behaviors are personal choices; environmental influences are conditions that make choices easier or harder.

stem: Sort each feature of a fictional neighborhood as a risk factor or a protective factor.
options: ["Risk factor", "Protective factor"]
rows: ["A recreation center with free programs", "A factory releasing smoke near homes", "No safe crossing near the school", "A community garden with fresh produce"]
rationale: Risk factors raise the chance of poor outcomes; protective factors support health.

stem: A fictional neighborhood has no safe places to play or exercise. How could this condition influence health?
options: ["Residents may have fewer chances to be active, which can affect fitness.", "It has no effect, since exercise is a purely personal choice.", "It only affects older residents and has no effect on kids.", "It guarantees that every resident will eventually have a serious disease."]
rationale: Conditions can make healthy choices harder without determining one person's outcome.

stem: Residents live near a clinic but have no safe way to get there at night. Which intervention is the most realistic and best justified?
options: ["Open a high-end spa near the clinic for residents to enjoy.", "Build a second clinic nearby, even though one is already close.", "Tell residents to travel at night despite any danger, since it is personal.", "Add better lighting and a night bus stop to make travel safe."]
rationale: A good intervention targets the actual barrier in the scenario.

stem: Which statement best explains how public health differs from healthcare?
options: ["Healthcare protects whole communities; public health treats individual patients.", "Public health only exists to respond to natural disasters.", "The two are identical and have the same goals and methods.", "Public health protects whole communities; healthcare mainly treats individuals."]
rationale: Public health works at the population level; healthcare focuses on individual patients.

stem: Which are functions of public-health agencies? Select all that apply.
options: ["Setting broken bones for individual patients", "Inspecting restaurants and water supplies", "Running vaccination clinics", "Teaching the public about health risks", "Performing heart surgeries", "Investigating the cause of outbreaks"]
rationale: Inspection, prevention, outbreak investigation, and education protect communities.

stem: Match each problem to the group most likely to respond.
options: ["Doctor or hospital", "Local health department", "CDC (federal)"]
rows: ["Tracking flu patterns across the whole country", "A child needs stitches after a fall", "Offering free flu shots at a county health fair", "Testing a town's water after several people become ill"]
rationale: Individual care goes to providers; local problems go to local departments; national tracking involves the CDC.

stem: Match each question to the part of STOP (Source, Timeliness, Objective, Proof) it checks.
options: ["Source", "Timeliness", "Objective", "Proof"]
rows: ["Is the author a recognized health expert?", "Does the page exist mainly to sell a product?", "Does it link to studies or data?", "Was the page updated recently?"]
rationale: STOP helps judge authority, timing, purpose, and evidence.

stem: Data show higher diabetes rates in Town X than in Town Y. What does the data alone show?
options: ["That the numbers must be mistaken because they differ", "That Town X's water is to blame for the gap", "That people in Town X choose worse foods", "A gap in outcomes, and the cause needs more information."]
rationale: A disparity shows a difference exists; it does not prove why.

stem: Which are common environmental health hazards? Select all that apply.
options: ["Very loud noise at concerts", "Clean air on a calm day", "Lead in drinking water", "Shade from a tree", "Wildfire smoke", "Heat waves"]
rationale: Smoke, contaminated water, loud noise, and extreme heat can all harm health.

stem: Match each example to hazard, exposure, or risk.
options: ["Hazard", "Exposure", "Risk"]
rows: ["Standing next to the speakers for hours", "The chance of permanent hearing loss", "Wildfire smoke drifting into town", "Loud speakers at a concert"]
rationale: A hazard can cause harm, exposure is contact with it, and risk is the likelihood and severity of harm.

stem: One worker is in the sun 15 minutes with sunscreen and shade. Another is out six hours at noon with none. Whose risk of sun damage is higher?
options: ["The first, because shade somehow makes sunburn more likely.", "The same, since both workers are out in the sun at some point.", "The second: stronger exposure, longer time, and no protection raise risk.", "Neither, because sunlight is never harmful to anyone's skin."]
rationale: Risk depends on intensity, duration, and protection, not just the hazard.

stem: The UV Index forecast for today is 9 (Very High). What is the best interpretation?
options: ["UV matters only on cloudy days, never on sunny days.", "Only people with dark skin need to worry about UV at all.", "Use sunscreen, shade, and cover-ups at midday.", "UV is low, so no sun protection is needed at all today."]
rationale: A very high UV Index calls for sun protection for everyone.

stem: A football practice is scheduled on an extreme heat day. Which protective behaviors are realistic? Select all that apply.
options: ["Check the heat forecast and adjust the schedule", "Add water breaks and shade", "Ignore heat warnings because practice must go on", "Shorten practice or lower the intensity", "Skip drinking water so players do not feel sluggish"]
rationale: Risk can be reduced with practical steps even when the hazard remains.

stem: A fictional energy drink ad uses extreme sports clips, loud music, and gamer influencers. Who is the intended audience?
options: ["Toddlers and preschoolers", "Hospital doctors and nurses", "Teens and young adults", "Retired adults over seventy"]
rationale: Visuals, music, and influencers show who the advertiser wants to reach.

stem: Match each ad line to the persuasive technique it uses.
options: ["Social proof", "Celebrity or influencer endorsement", "Scarcity", "Fear"]
rows: ["\"Last chance, the deal ends tonight!\"", "\"If you skip this, you'll fall behind everyone.\"", "A famous gamer sips the drink in a video", "\"9 out of 10 teens choose it!\""]
rationale: Ads use crowd appeal, famous faces, urgency, and fear to persuade.

stem: A cereal ad shows a happy family at breakfast but never states that the cereal is healthy. What is the implied message?
options: ["That it is made without any ingredients at all", "That it has the lowest sugar of any cereal", "That there is no message because no claim is stated", "That eating it leads to a happy family morning"]
rationale: Ads can imply benefits without making an explicit claim.

stem: Many students believe "everybody skips breakfast," but a survey shows most students eat it. How can this belief affect behavior?
options: ["It only affects people who already skip breakfast.", "It only matters if the belief happens to be accurate.", "It cannot, because only measured facts ever influence people.", "People often copy what seems normal, even if wrong."]
rationale: Perceived norms can shape behavior even when they are inaccurate.

stem: A soda company posts ads for teens on many apps every day. How could the repeated messages affect community health behavior?
options: ["It guarantees that every single teen will buy the drink.", "They can make it seem normal and appealing to many people.", "It only affects people who already liked the drink beforehand.", "Repetition has no effect, because people decide only using facts and prices."]
rationale: Repeated exposure can shape norms across a community without determining any one person's choice.

stem: Which is the clearest, most specific community-health problem statement?
options: ["Many students skip sunscreen outdoors, risking sunburn.", "Students' health is not as good as it could possibly be.", "Our community should be much healthier than it currently is.", "There is a lot of sunshine in the world around us every day."]
rationale: A clear problem names who is affected and what the harm is.

stem: For the problem of students skipping sunscreen, which intervention is the most specific and realistic?
options: ["A general goal to make everyone at the school healthier", "A sun-safety campaign with posters and sunscreen stations at outdoor events", "A request that students simply care more about their skin", "A school-wide ban on all outdoor events during the spring"]
rationale: A good intervention is specific, feasible, and linked to the problem.

stem: To get more shade structures built at a city park, which is the best audience for an advocacy message?
options: ["Anyone who happens to scroll past a social media post", "The parks department, which can decide and fund it", "A famous celebrity who has no connection to the park", "A group of students who already agree with the request"]
rationale: Advocacy targets people with the power to act.

stem: Which is a clear call to action?
options: ["We hope that people will think more about sun safety.", "Shade is important for the health of everyone at the park.", "We ask the city to install shade structures at the park by next summer.", "Someone should really do something about the sun here soon."]
rationale: A call to action names who should do what and by when.

stem: Which could show that a sun-safety campaign worked? Select all that apply.
options: ["The number of flyers handed out", "A survey of sunscreen use before and after the campaign", "The share of students using shade at a follow-up event", "How bright the poster colors are"]
rationale: Success is measured by changes in behavior or outcomes, not effort or appearance.

stem: Match each fictional example to tolerance, physical dependence, or addiction.
options: ["Tolerance", "Physical dependence", "Addiction (substance use disorder)"]
rows: ["A patient on prescribed medicine has withdrawal when it stops but no craving or compulsive use", "Needing a bigger dose over time to feel the same effect", "Using a substance compulsively despite damage to school and relationships", "Feeling sick and shaky when a medication is suddenly stopped"]
rationale: Tolerance and dependence are body adaptations; addiction is compulsive use despite harm.

stem: Which describe ways psychoactive substances can affect the brain or behavior? Select all that apply.
options: ["They can alter chemical signals between brain cells", "They only change behavior in people who already have a disorder", "They can change mood and affect memory", "They can slow reaction time and reduce coordination", "They affect the body only and never the brain"]
rationale: Substances change brain signaling and can affect reaction time, coordination, mood, and memory.

stem: Which statements about the risk of substance-use problems are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: ["Genes, stress, and easy access can all add to risk", "Early first use is linked with higher risk", "A single risk factor always leads to addiction", "Strong connections to caring adults can lower risk", "Addiction means the person has weak character"]
rationale: Risk comes from many interacting factors, and addiction is a health condition, not a character flaw.

stem: Which statement helps explain why teens may take more risks than adults?
options: ["Teens do not feel rewards as strongly as adults do.", "Teen brains finished developing years ago, so choices explain it all.", "Impulse control is still maturing but rewards feel strong.", "Adults and teens have identical brain development at all times."]
rationale: Reward-seeking is strong while self-control is still maturing during adolescence.

stem: Which source would best support a claim about how nicotine affects the teen brain?
options: ["A popular post by an anonymous online account", "A CDC or NIH page on teen nicotine use", "A store website that is selling vaping products", "A classmate's strong opinion about nicotine"]
rationale: Credible claims are backed by expert, evidence-based organizations.

stem: Why is nicotine especially worrying for teenagers?
options: ["Teen bodies break nicotine down so fast it cannot affect them.", "Nicotine is only a concern for people over the age of thirty.", "Nicotine only causes harm after decades of regular use.", "It is highly addictive and can disrupt attention in teens."]
rationale: The developing brain is more vulnerable to nicotine's effects and to dependence.

stem: Which are health risks linked to tobacco or vaping? Select all that apply.
options: ["Higher risk of heart and lung disease over time", "Nicotine dependence", "Better sleep from nicotine", "Trouble with concentration and mood", "Stronger lungs from inhaling aerosol", "Coughing and airway irritation"]
rationale: Nicotine, aerosol, and smoke are linked to dependence, airway irritation, brain effects, and long-term disease.

stem: Match each influence to the category it shows.
options: ["Marketing", "Product design or flavors", "Peer norms"]
rows: ["Thinking \"all my friends do it\"", "Devices shaped like everyday objects that are easy to hide", "Ads with bright colors and teen models", "Sweet dessert and mint flavors"]
rationale: Marketing, flavors and design, and perceived norms all shape youth nicotine use.

stem: Which of these claims are inaccurate? Select all that apply.
options: ["A product on the shelf has been proven safe for teens.", "Aerosol can carry nicotine and ultrafine particles.", "Flavored products cannot addict anyone.", "Vape aerosol is only harmless flavoring.", "Cigarette smoke contains many toxic chemicals."]
rationale: Aerosol is not just flavoring, flavors do not remove nicotine, and being sold does not mean safe for youth.

stem: Which counter-message is accurate and suited to teens?
options: ["\"Vapes are safe because they do not produce any smoke.\"", "\"Only people with weak willpower ever get addicted to nicotine.\"", "\"One puff will ruin your life forever, so be terrified.\"", "\"Flavored vapes still deliver nicotine, which is addictive. Check the FDA.\""]
rationale: Good counter-messages are accurate, avoid exaggeration, and point to credible sources.

stem: Which are short-term effects of alcohol that can affect safety or decisions? Select all that apply.
options: ["Gaps in memory", "Better coordination on the road", "Improved focus on schoolwork", "Slower reaction time", "Blurred judgment", "Trouble with balance"]
rationale: Alcohol impairs reaction time, judgment, balance, and memory.

stem: Which statements explain why alcohol affects people differently? Select all that apply.
options: ["Some medications interact with alcohol", "Someone who feels okay can safely drive", "Two drinks affect everyone the same way every time", "Drinking fast raises impairment more than drinking slowly", "Smaller body size can mean a stronger effect"]
rationale: Body size, speed, and medications change the effect, and feeling fine does not mean being unimpaired.

stem: A fictional teen's driver has been drinking. Match each statement to the decision-making step it shows.
options: ["Define the problem", "List options", "Think about consequences", "Choose the safest decision"]
rows: ["I will call a family member to pick me up", "A crash could cause injuries, arrests, and lost trust", "I could call a family member, wait for a sober driver, or use a ride service", "A friend offers to drive me home after drinking"]
rationale: A structured process moves from the problem to options, consequences, and the safest choice.

stem: Eli (fictional) is at a party and his driver has been drinking. Which response best weighs alternatives and consequences?
options: ["Puts off deciding anything and hopes everything works out fine", "Accepts the first ride offered because it is the quickest way home", "Compares a sober ride or a family call and picks the safest", "Goes with whatever most of the people in the group decide to do"]
rationale: Safer alternatives and their consequences should be compared before acting.

stem: Which are signs that someone who drank alcohol needs emergency help right away? Select all that apply.
options: ["Passed out and cannot be woken", "Seizure", "Laughing more than usual", "Feeling a little warm but speaking clearly", "Pale, bluish, or clammy skin"]
rationale: Seizures, bluish skin, and unresponsiveness can mean alcohol poisoning; call emergency services.

stem: Which are ways marijuana can affect functioning or safety? Select all that apply.
options: ["It has no effect on the brain", "Short-term memory problems", "Trouble concentrating on tasks", "Altered judgment about risks", "It reliably improves driving skill", "Slowed reflexes when driving or biking"]
rationale: Cannabis can affect attention, reaction time, memory, and judgment.

stem: Sort each example as prescribed use or misuse.
options: ["Prescribed use", "Misuse"]
rows: ["Using an inhaler exactly as the doctor directed", "Taking a double dose for faster relief", "Using a parent's leftover pain medicine for a sprain", "Taking antibiotics as prescribed until they are finished"]
rationale: Using someone else's medication or more than prescribed is misuse.

stem: Why are opioids so dangerous in an overdose?
options: ["They make the heart beat too fast to keep working.", "They only harm people who have used them for years.", "They are only dangerous when mixed with food.", "They can slow or stop breathing in a large dose."]
rationale: Opioids depress breathing, which makes overdose life-threatening.

stem: A fictional friend says a blue pill from a stranger is "just a pain pill." Why can't anyone tell it is safe by looking?
options: ["Real pills always carry a logo that proves they are genuine.", "Pills with natural-sounding ingredients are always safe to take.", "Fake pills can look real but contain fentanyl.", "Pills sold at a cheap price are always the weaker versions."]
rationale: You cannot tell what is in a pill by looking, and counterfeit pills can be deadly.

stem: Which are key parts of responding to a suspected opioid overdose? Select all that apply.
options: ["Let them sleep and check back in the morning", "Call 911 immediately", "Give them a cold shower or a hot drink", "Stay with the person until help arrives", "Give naloxone if it is on hand"]
rationale: Naloxone can temporarily reverse an overdose, but emergency medical help is still needed.

stem: Sort each fictional situation as direct or indirect pressure.
options: ["Direct pressure", "Indirect pressure"]
rows: ["You see a post that makes drinking look fun and normal", "A classmate says, \"Come on, everyone is doing it.\"", "A friend keeps pushing a drink into your hand", "Everyone at the table is vaping and you notice"]
rationale: Direct pressure is said out loud; indirect pressure comes from the situation and social cues.

stem: Match each response to passive, aggressive, or assertive communication.
options: ["Passive", "Aggressive", "Assertive"]
rows: ["Avoids eye contact and says, \"sure, I guess\"", "Goes along quietly so nobody gets upset", "Says calmly, \"No thanks, I'm not interested,\" and steps away", "Shoves the person and shouts at them"]
rationale: Assertive communication is clear and respectful; passive gives in and aggressive attacks.

stem: Which are effective refusal or exit strategies? Select all that apply.
options: ["Asking a friend to leave together", "Agreeing now to avoid a fight", "Leaving and texting a trusted adult for a ride", "Saying a firm \"No\" and offering another plan", "Giving a long, nervous explanation of why not"]
rationale: Firm refusals, exits, and allies work; long excuses and giving in do not.

stem: Which refusal uses strong body language and concise words?
options: ["Giggling and repeating \"maybe, I dunno\" over and over", "Whispering a long excuse while looking away", "Standing tall: \"No thanks, not for me.\"", "Crossing arms and loudly mocking the person"]
rationale: Confident posture and a brief, clear statement make refusal more effective.

stem: A fictional teen finds a friend who took pills and is hard to wake. What is the best action?
options: ["Keep quiet so the friend avoids getting in trouble", "Wait to see if the friend feels better later", "Call 911 and get a trusted adult immediately", "Try to handle it alone so adults never find out"]
rationale: Safety comes before secrecy; some situations need emergency help immediately.

stem: Match each description to the correct term.
options: ["Probability", "House edge", "Gambler's fallacy"]
rows: ["How likely a chance event is, shown as a number", "Thinking a color is \"due\" after a long streak on a wheel", "The advantage that makes a game pay out less than the true odds", "The average share of money wagered that the business keeps"]
rationale: Probability measures chance, house edge is the game's built-in advantage, and the gambler's fallacy is a false belief about streaks.

stem: A fair roulette-style wheel lands on red six times in a row. Which statement is true about the next spin?
options: ["The wheel must be broken, so nothing can be predicted at all.", "Red is now certain to continue, because it is on a streak.", "It has the same chance of red or black each spin.", "Black is now more likely, since the wheel has to balance out."]
rationale: Streaks do not change the odds of the next independent spin.

stem: A fair spinner has 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5. What is the probability of landing on 3?
rationale: One of five equally likely outcomes is a 3, so the probability is 1/5.

stem: A game costs $5 to play. There is a 1-in-20 chance to win $60 and otherwise you win nothing. What is the expected result per play, on average?
options: ["Break even ($0)", "A loss of $2 per play", "A gain of $55 per play", "A gain of $3 per play"]
rationale: Expected value is (1/20 x $60) - $5 = -$2, so players lose on average.

stem: Why do gambling businesses make money over time even though some customers win?
options: ["Customers who study a game long enough always beat the odds.", "The business secretly decides which customers will win and lose.", "Winners are required to return their money the following day.", "Payouts are set below the true odds, so the business keeps a share overall."]
rationale: House advantage guarantees an average profit for the business over many bets.

stem: Match each fictional example to the term it shows.
options: ["Variable reinforcement", "Near miss", "Chasing losses", "Tolerance"]
rows: ["Needing riskier bets to feel the same thrill", "Prizes from loot boxes arrive at random times", "A scratch ticket is missing just one matching symbol", "Doubling a bet after a loss to try to recover"]
rationale: These are key patterns that keep reward systems engaged and keep people gambling.

stem: Why do random, unpredictable prizes, like those in loot boxes, keep people playing?
options: ["Unpredictable rewards trigger a stronger, longer dopamine response.", "Dopamine is released only at the moment a player loses money.", "Predictable rewards cause the stronger and longer dopamine response.", "Players always know exactly when the next prize is coming."]
rationale: Variable reinforcement produces a strong, persistent reward response.

stem: Which statement describes the brain development gap in teenagers?
options: ["Both brain systems are completely finished developing by thirteen.", "The prefrontal cortex matures completely before the reward circuits do.", "Teens lack reward circuits, which is why they take chances.", "Reward-seeking circuits mature earlier than the self-control of the prefrontal cortex."]
rationale: Reward-seeking develops before impulse control and judgment finish maturing.

stem: Why does that gap raise a teen's vulnerability to gambling and other addictions?
options: ["Teens feel no rewards, so they keep searching for bigger ones.", "Teens always grasp the odds, which makes them completely safe.", "Teens are worse at reading rules than adults are, so they lose more.", "Strong reward-seeking and maturing self-control make quitting hard."]
rationale: The gap between reward drive and self-control increases the risk of addictive patterns.

stem: Which can raise a person's vulnerability to problem gambling? Select all that apply.
options: ["Understanding how odds really work", "Close support from caring adults", "Playing gambling-style games at a young age", "A strong desire for thrills and rewards", "Acting without thinking (impulsivity)"]
rationale: Impulsivity, thrill-seeking, and early exposure raise risk; support and knowing the odds are protective.

stem: Match each fictional ad line to the technique it uses.
options: ["Sign-up bonus or \"risk-free\" bet", "Celebrity or influencer promotion", "Streak or loyalty reward", "Social proof"]
rows: ["\"Keep your streak alive for bonus bets!\"", "\"Get a $200 bonus when you sign up today!\"", "A famous quarterback says, \"I trust this app.\"", "\"Join the millions of fans who bet on game day.\""]
rationale: Bonuses, famous faces, rewards for staying active, and crowd appeal are common betting marketing tactics.

stem: Which are persuasive techniques used in sports-betting ads? Select all that apply.
options: ["Free bet offers for new customers", "Star athletes promoting the app", "Explaining how the house edge works", "Rewards for betting several days in a row", "\"Risk-free\" first bet language", "Posting the real chance of losing in bold type"]
rationale: Ads highlight excitement and rewards and rarely show the odds or the house edge.

stem: A fictional betting promo uses esports clips, popular streamers, and trending slang. Which audience is it most likely aiming for?
options: ["Professional poker players", "Toddlers and preschoolers", "Teens and young adults", "Older retired adults"]
rationale: Content, platforms, and language show who an ad wants to reach.

stem: How can nonstop sports-betting ads during games normalize gambling for young people?
options: ["It makes betting look like something almost no one does.", "It teaches viewers the real odds and risks of every bet.", "Betting shown beside fandom and stars seems like a normal part of sports.", "It has no effect, because young people cannot legally bet."]
rationale: Repeated exposure shapes what feels normal, even for people who cannot yet bet.

stem: Why is a "bonus bet" not truly free money?
options: ["A bonus bet can never lose any money at any time.", "The company pays every loss with no limits or conditions.", "The bonus changes the odds in the customer's favor.", "Bonuses come with conditions, so winnings often must be wagered first."]
rationale: The wording hides the conditions and keeps the player betting.

stem: Which could be warning signs of problem gambling? Select all that apply.
options: ["Betting more to chase lost money", "Choosing other activities over betting", "Walking away after a set limit every time", "Hiding gambling from family and friends", "Falling behind on schoolwork or chores", "Being preoccupied with gambling"]
rationale: Preoccupation, secrecy, chasing losses, and neglecting responsibilities are warning signs.

stem: Dee (fictional) is invited to join a sports bracket pool. Match each statement to the decision-making step.
options: ["Identify the problem", "List options", "Think about consequences", "Make the decision"]
rows: ["Join, decline, or suggest watching the game together instead", "Dee is asked to put money into a sports bracket pool", "Losing money, continued pressure, and damaged friendships", "Dee says no and suggests watching together"]
rationale: A decision-making model moves from the problem to options, consequences, and a choice.

stem: Which is the clearest refusal when a friend pushes you to join a betting game?
options: ["\"No thanks, I'm not in. Want to grab pizza instead?\"", "\"I would join, but I would probably get caught.\"", "\"Maybe some other time, I guess, if I happen to have money.\"", "\"That's a ridiculous thing to do and you should stop!\""]
rationale: A clear, calm "no" with an alternative is an effective refusal.

stem: Where can someone find help for problem gambling? Select all that apply.
options: ["Borrow money from friends to cover the losses", "Keep it secret and try to win the money back", "A parent or trusted adult", "ncpgambling.org and the helpline at 1-800-522-4700", "A school counselor"]
rationale: Counselors, trusted adults, and the helpline offer support; secrecy and borrowing make things worse.

stem: Sort each consequence of problem gambling as financial or social.
options: ["Financial consequence", "Social consequence"]
rows: ["Pulling away from friends and activities", "Arguments and broken trust with family", "Running out of money meant for lunch or bills", "Debt from borrowing to place more bets"]
rationale: Problem gambling harms both money and relationships.

stem: A fictional data card says: "In a sample of 20 teen bike crashes with head injuries, 14 riders were not wearing helmets." What is the main finding?
options: ["Only a few of the injured riders were without helmets.", "Helmets caused most of the head injuries in the sample.", "Most riders with head injuries in the sample were not wearing helmets.", "Most riders with head injuries had been wearing helmets."]
rationale: 14 of 20 is most of the sample. Summarizing a data card means stating what the numbers show.

stem: Which source would give the most trustworthy statistics on teen injuries?
options: ["A video review of a safety gadget", "A classmate's guess at the numbers", "CDC or NHTSA injury-data pages", "A viral post that lists no source"]
rationale: Credible statistics come from agencies that publish their data and methods.

stem: How does a seat belt help protect you in a crash?
options: ["It keeps you from hitting the dashboard or leaving the car.", "It only helps in slow crashes under ten miles per hour.", "It makes crashes less likely by keeping the car steady.", "It protects the car's seat more than it protects the passenger."]
rationale: Seat belts hold people in place so crash forces are absorbed by stronger parts of the body.

stem: How does a bike helmet help protect the brain in a fall?
options: ["Its foam cushions the impact on the head.", "It matters only for riders on very busy roads.", "It keeps riders from falling off the bike at all.", "It protects equally well when worn loose on top of the head."]
rationale: A properly fitted helmet reduces the force that reaches the head and brain.

stem: Sort each statement as a myth or a fact.
options: ["Myth", "Fact"]
rows: ["\"Wearing a seat belt lowers the risk of dying in a crash.\"", "\"Seat belts are only needed on long highway trips.\"", "\"Many injuries are predictable and can be prevented.\"", "\"Experienced riders do not need helmets.\""]
rationale: Protective habits help in every trip, and many injuries are preventable.

stem: You see a teen collapse in a hallway and not breathe normally. What are the first two steps of the Chain of Survival?
options: ["Give rescue breaths for two minutes before calling anyone", "Recognize cardiac arrest and call 911", "Carry the person outside, then call a relative", "Give water, then wait to see if the person wakes up"]
rationale: Recognizing cardiac arrest and calling 911 come first.

stem: Which are steps or links in the Chain of Survival? Select all that apply.
options: ["Push hard and fast on the chest", "Wait for the person to recover on their own", "Move them to a bed first", "Use an AED when it arrives", "Call 911 immediately", "Continue until EMS takes over"]
rationale: The chain is recognize, call 911, compress, use an AED, and hand off to EMS.

stem: For hands-only CPR on an adult, where do the heels of your hands go?
options: ["On the left shoulder, close to the collarbone and neck", "Over the stomach, just under the bottom of the ribs", "In the center of the chest, hands stacked", "On the upper back, between the two shoulder blades"]
rationale: Compressions go on the center of the chest.

stem: Which tempo fits the compression rate for hands-only CPR?
options: ["As fast as you possibly can, around 200 a minute", "A steady beat of 100 to 120 compressions a minute", "A slow, careful pace of about 40 compressions a minute", "Fast for a while, then a long pause, then fast again"]
rationale: A steady rate of 100 to 120 per minute keeps blood moving effectively.

stem: Which describes hands-only CPR best?
options: ["Pressing on the chest for one minute, then stopping to wait", "Pushing hard and fast on the chest with no rescue breaths", "Gentle chest taps every few seconds until help arrives", "Giving rescue breaths only, with no chest compressions at all"]
rationale: Hands-only CPR is continuous chest compressions until help arrives.

stem: Put the AED steps in order. Match each step to when it happens.
options: ["First", "Second", "Third", "Fourth"]
rows: ["Place the pads on bare skin where the pictures show", "Restart chest compressions when the AED tells you to", "Press the power button and listen to the voice prompts", "Tell everyone to stand clear while the AED checks"]
rationale: The sequence is power on, pads on, stand clear, then resume CPR as prompted.

stem: The AED says, "Shock delivered. Begin CPR." What should you do?
options: ["Wait ten minutes before touching the person", "Take off the pads and walk away", "Wait until the person sits up by themselves", "Begin chest compressions right away"]
rationale: CPR continues after a shock until prompted otherwise or EMS takes over.

stem: How do CPR and an AED fit together during an emergency?
options: ["An AED makes chest compressions unnecessary once the pads are on.", "CPR begins only after the AED has failed several times.", "Using either one by itself is always enough to save someone.", "CPR moves blood while the AED checks the heart."]
rationale: CPR, the AED, and calling 911 together make up the response most likely to save a life.

stem: Myth: "Hospitals let a registered donor die so they can use the organs." Which fact corrects it?
options: ["Hospitals only treat donors if their organs are in good shape.", "Doctors work to save every patient's life first, donor or not.", "Registering signs a contract that ends normal medical treatment.", "Registered donors are placed at the back of the line for care."]
rationale: Being a registered donor does not change the care a person receives.

stem: Myth: "You must be young and perfectly healthy to be an organ donor." Which fact corrects it?
options: ["Only people under twenty-five can ever become donors.", "People of many ages and health conditions can register as donors.", "Donors must pass a fitness test before they can sign up.", "Only people with no medical history at all can register."]
rationale: Age and many health conditions do not automatically rule out registering as a donor.

stem: In a walking test, students take longer to react when they are also texting. What does this show?
options: ["Only loud noises, and never phones, can slow down reaction time.", "Distraction slows reaction time, so a person moves farther before reacting.", "Texting sharpens attention by keeping the mind busy and engaged.", "Reaction time stays the same no matter what else is going on."]
rationale: Divided attention measurably delays response, which raises crash risk.

stem: Match each example to the type of distraction it shows.
options: ["Visual", "Manual", "Cognitive"]
rows: ["Holding a phone with one hand while steering", "Glancing at a map app instead of the road", "Watching a video on a screen while crossing a street", "Thinking about tomorrow's test while driving"]
rationale: Distractions can take eyes, hands, or attention away from the task.

stem: Why is using a phone while driving more dangerous than most other distractions?
options: ["It only takes the driver's eyes off the road for a moment.", "It is risky only at very high speeds on highways.", "It is only dangerous when the driver is not talking.", "It takes eyes, hands, and attention off driving."]
rationale: Phone use combines visual, manual, and cognitive distraction.

stem: Which are healthy technology habits that support safety? Select all that apply.
options: ["Checking messages at stop lights while driving", "Posting a live location story every few minutes", "Turning on a driving mode that silences alerts", "Looking up before stepping into a crosswalk", "Muting group chats while riding a bike", "Keeping live location private from strangers"]
rationale: Safe habits limit distractions and protect privacy.

stem: Which is a specific, realistic safety commitment for a fictional student?
options: ["\"I will be a better and safer person this year.\"", "\"I will never carry a phone anywhere again in my life.\"", "\"I will use my phone only when it feels safe enough.\"", "\"I will mute my notifications before I ride.\""]
rationale: A strong commitment names a specific action and is realistic to follow.

stem: Match each job to the macronutrient that does it.
options: ["Carbohydrates", "Protein", "Fat"]
rows: ["Stores energy and helps cells work properly", "Gives quick, steady energy to the brain and muscles", "Found mostly in pasta, oats, and bananas", "Helps build muscle and repair tissue"]
rationale: Carbohydrates fuel the body, protein builds and repairs, and fat stores energy and supports cells.

stem: Which foods are mostly protein? Select all that apply.
options: ["Lean turkey", "Potatoes", "Fish", "Butter", "Cottage cheese"]
rationale: Fish, turkey, and cottage cheese are protein-rich; potatoes are mostly carbohydrate and butter is mostly fat.

stem: Which fictional dinner best matches the MyPlate proportions?
options: ["A plate with only mashed potatoes and gravy", "Baked fish, quinoa, carrots, a pear, and yogurt", "A bowl of cereal with nothing else on the table", "Three tacos with extra cheese and a large sweet drink"]
rationale: A MyPlate meal includes fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, and dairy in balanced proportions.

stem: Which statement about MyPlate is accurate?
options: ["It shows balance and variety across food groups as a flexible guide.", "It requires every meal to match its picture exactly.", "It lists the only foods that people are allowed to eat.", "It is a calorie-restricted plan for losing weight."]
rationale: MyPlate shows balance across food groups rather than one perfect meal.

stem: Which statement about micronutrients is accurate?
options: ["They supply the main fuel that the body uses for energy.", "Only supplement pills can provide them to the body.", "They are another word for the proteins in food.", "Vitamins and minerals help the body in small amounts."]
rationale: Micronutrients are needed in small amounts and come from a variety of foods.

stem: Match each description to the part of the nutrition facts label.
options: ["Serving size", "Calories", "% Daily Value", "Added sugars"]
rows: ["The amount of energy one serving provides", "The amount the label's numbers are based on, such as 3/4 cup", "Sugar added during processing, listed on its own line", "How much a serving contributes to daily needs, shown as a percent"]
rationale: Each part of the label answers a different question about the food.

stem: A nutrient lists 3% Daily Value per serving. How is that generally described?
options: ["Low (5% or less)", "High (20% or more)", "Perfect for one meal", "Impossible to interpret"]
rationale: A rough guide: 5% or less is low and 20% or more is high.

stem: Yogurt A has 18 g added sugar per serving and Yogurt B has 7 g, with the same serving size. Which statement is accurate?
options: ["Yogurt A has less added sugar.", "Both have the same added sugar.", "Labels cannot be compared across different brands.", "Yogurt B has less added sugar per serving."]
rationale: Comparing the same serving size on both labels shows which has less added sugar.

stem: A box lists 3 servings of 120 calories each. A student eats the whole box. How many calories, and what does serving size mean?
options: ["360 calories; serving size is the amount everyone must eat.", "360 calories; serving size is only a reference.", "40 calories; labels list only one-third of a serving.", "120 calories; the label always lists the whole box's total."]
rationale: Portion size is what a person actually eats; serving size is a standard amount for comparison.

stem: Match each visual reference to what it can help estimate.
options: ["Palm", "Fist", "Cupped hand", "Thumb"]
rows: ["About a tablespoon of oil or butter", "About a handful of nuts or trail mix", "About a cup of rice or cereal", "About one serving of fish"]
rationale: Hand-based references are a practical estimating tool, not a strict rule.

stem: Match each description to the FITT component.
options: ["Frequency", "Intensity", "Time", "Type"]
rows: ["Three days each week", "A hard pace that makes it difficult to talk", "Forty-five minutes per workout", "Cycling, dancing, or lifting weights"]
rationale: FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time, and Type.

stem: Nia (fictional) cycles at an easy pace for 15 minutes on 3 days a week. Which change increases the Time component?
options: ["Cycling on 5 days a week instead of 3", "Swimming laps instead of cycling", "Adding hill sprints to the ride", "Cycling for 30 minutes each time"]
rationale: Time is how long; the other choices change frequency, intensity, and type.

stem: Which plan includes all four FITT components?
options: ["Swim at a moderate pace for 30 minutes, 3 days a week", "Swim for 30 minutes on 3 days a week at no particular effort level", "Swim at a moderate pace on 3 days a week as time allows", "Swim at a moderate pace for 30 minutes whenever there is time"]
rationale: A FITT plan names how often, how hard, how long, and what kind of activity.

stem: A student can talk but cannot sing during a jog. Using the talk test, what is the intensity?
options: ["Vigorous, because they can only say a few words", "Moderate, because talking is possible but singing is not", "Light, because they can sing the whole song", "It cannot be judged using the talk test"]
rationale: If you can talk but not sing, the activity is moderate.

stem: A student rates effort 8 out of 10 and can say only a few words. What does this suggest?
options: ["Vigorous, because they can barely talk", "Light, because they can sing along easily", "It is impossible to judge from an effort rating", "Moderate, because the effort rating is only a 4"]
rationale: A high effort rating and difficulty talking show vigorous intensity.

stem: Match each example to the marketing technique it uses.
options: ["Health halo (front-label claim)", "Influencer promotion", "Dramatic before/after claim"]
rows: ["\"Made with whole grains!\" on a box high in added sugar", "\"Light and natural!\" on a cookie package", "A fitness star wearing the brand and posting a promo code", "A \"body transformation\" in thirty days"]
rationale: Front-label claims, influencer promotion, and dramatic before/after images are common patterns.

stem: A drink says "Real fruit juice!" on the front, but the label shows 24 g of added sugar. Which technique is this?
options: ["A health halo: a front claim hides the real label.", "A scarcity claim, because the drink is a limited item", "Social proof, because many shoppers already buy it", "A doctor's recommendation printed on the bottle"]
rationale: The front claim draws attention while the added sugar is on the full label.

stem: Which are common patterns in social-media fitness marketing? Select all that apply.
options: ["Promises of quick or extreme transformations", "Balanced advice that cites its sources", "Before/after photos that promise results in days", "Influencers promoting supplements with discount codes", "Information reviewed by a medical expert"]
rationale: These patterns grab attention without giving reliable evidence.

stem: Why should a trendy workout claim be verified with a credible source?
options: ["If a claim goes viral, it has already been fact-checked by others.", "Workout claims on social media must always be complete and accurate.", "Marketing grabs attention fast, while credible sources show the real evidence.", "Trendy claims are always tested by independent experts first."]
rationale: Credible sources, like a dietitian or public health organization, provide the real picture.

stem: Which are credible sources for checking a fitness or nutrition claim? Select all that apply.
options: ["A public health organization such as the CDC", "An unsigned post from a stranger", "A registered dietitian", "A creator's promo-code page", "A doctor or pediatrician"]
rationale: Experts and public health organizations are credible; sellers and anonymous posts are not.

stem: Which goal includes all five SMART components?
options: ["I will drink a glass of water with lunch on 5 school days each week.", "I will drink water at every moment of every day for the rest of my life.", "I will drink more water and feel a lot better pretty soon, hopefully.", "I will drink a glass of water with lunch 5 days a week for 3 weeks to stay focused."]
rationale: The goal names an action, a number, a realistic target, a reason, and a time frame.

stem: Match each phrase from a goal to the SMART component it shows.
options: ["Specific", "Measurable", "Achievable", "Relevant", "Time-bound"]
rows: ["\"over the next 3 weeks\"", "\"on 5 school days a week\"", "\"to have more energy for practice\"", "\"swap one soda for water\"", "\"using the water fountain by my class\""]
rationale: Each part of a SMART goal answers a different question.

stem: Which is a habit-based goal?
options: ["Change my body to look like an athlete online.", "Drop 15 pounds before the summer starts, no matter what.", "Walk 15 minutes after dinner on four evenings.", "Stay under a strict number of calories each day."]
rationale: Habit-based goals focus on actions, not weight, calories, or body size.

stem: Which are realistic barriers to a goal of doing 20 minutes of activity before school? Select all that apply.
options: ["No safe place to exercise near home", "Having a clear plan", "Telling a friend about the goal", "Not enough time before the bus", "Feeling too tired in the morning"]
rationale: A barrier is something that could get in the way of the goal.

stem: Barrier: "I forget to do my activity after school." Which strategy fits?
options: ["Give up because it is too hard to remember", "Set a phone reminder and lay out clothes", "Do the activity only when you happen to remember", "Wait until summer when there is more free time"]
rationale: A strategy directly addresses the barrier.

stem: Sort each statement about puberty as a myth or a fact.
options: ["Myth", "Fact"]
rows: ["Growth spurts start at different ages for different people.", "Mood changes and new feelings can be a normal part of puberty.", "A person can skip puberty by eating the right foods.", "Puberty happens on the same exact schedule for every person."]
rationale: Puberty timing varies widely, and changes are physical and emotional.

stem: Leo (fictional) has not yet had the growth spurt some classmates have had. Which statement is most accurate?
options: ["His body will probably skip growth changes altogether.", "He must have a health problem that needs treatment.", "Timing varies from person to person and is normal.", "Everyone should grow at exactly the same time as each other."]
rationale: There is a wide, normal range for when puberty begins and how fast it goes.

stem: Which changes can happen during puberty? Select all that apply.
options: ["New friendships and interests", "Puberty ends at the same age for everyone", "Stronger or changing emotions", "Hormone changes", "Changes in height and body shape", "Emotions stop changing completely"]
rationale: Puberty involves physical, hormonal, emotional, and social changes.

stem: Which is the best place to get a trustworthy answer about body changes?
options: ["A social media post from a stranger who is very sure", "An advertisement for a product that claims to help", "Advice that a classmate overheard somewhere", "A doctor, the school nurse, or a site like the CDC"]
rationale: Reliable information comes from health professionals and recognized health organizations.

stem: Which are signs of a reliable health website? Select all that apply.
options: ["It links to its medical sources", "It names its authors or experts", "It says \"doctors hate this\" with no proof", "It asks you to buy something right away"]
rationale: Credible sites show who wrote them and where the facts come from.

stem: Sort each characteristic as healthy or unhealthy in a relationship.
options: ["Healthy", "Unhealthy"]
rows: ["Support during hard times", "Teasing or insulting someone to keep them down", "Listening and taking turns", "Checking someone's phone and deciding who they see"]
rationale: Healthy relationships have respect and support; control and put-downs are unhealthy.

stem: Which are warning signs of an unhealthy relationship? Select all that apply.
options: ["Choosing different hobbies", "Constant put-downs", "Saying \"no\" respectfully", "Threats or bullying", "Guilt-tripping to get one's way", "Cutting someone off from friends"]
rationale: Isolation, threats, put-downs, and guilt-tripping are warning signs; differences and respectful limits are normal.

stem: Which statement about consent is accurate?
options: ["Not saying no counts as a yes every time.", "Saying yes once means yes forever after that.", "Consent is freely given and can be taken back.", "Pushing someone with guilt is okay if they finally agree."]
rationale: Consent must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time.

stem: Which statement describes a personal boundary?
options: ["A rule that only people in couples need to follow", "A threat meant to control what other people do", "A limit that only counts if the other person approves", "A limit someone sets about what they are okay with"]
rationale: Boundaries apply in every relationship and others should respect them.

stem: A friend keeps borrowing a student's things without asking. Which statement sets a boundary clearly and respectfully?
options: ["\"I feel annoyed when you borrow my things. Please ask first.\"", "\"You are so selfish and nobody likes you.\"", "\"Fine, take it, I guess nothing I want matters.\"", "\"I will stop talking to you altogether from now on, for real.\""]
rationale: A clear, respectful boundary names the feeling, the situation, and what is needed.

stem: Sort each way as one that can or cannot spread HIV.
options: ["Can spread HIV", "Cannot spread HIV"]
rows: ["Sharing a drinking glass", "Sharing needles for injections", "Shaking hands", "Certain body fluids during sexual contact"]
rationale: HIV spreads only through certain body fluids; it does not spread through casual contact.

stem: Which statement about STIs is accurate?
options: ["STIs can only be passed through casual contact like hugging.", "Many STIs have no symptoms, so testing matters.", "STIs always cause obvious symptoms right away.", "Only one kind of STI exists, and it is always curable."]
rationale: Many STIs have no symptoms, which is why testing matters for anyone who is sexually active.

stem: Which are prevention methods for STIs? Select all that apply.
options: ["Abstinence", "Getting tested regularly", "Condoms used correctly every time (they reduce, but do not eliminate, risk)", "Birth control pills alone (they prevent pregnancy, not STIs)", "Showering after contact", "Vaccines such as the HPV vaccine"]
rationale: Abstinence, vaccination, testing, and condoms help; showering and birth control pills do not protect against STIs.

stem: Which method has no risk of sexually transmitted infection?
options: ["Getting tested, which finds infections but does not prevent them", "Getting vaccinated, which covers only some infections", "Using condoms every time, which still leaves some risk", "Abstinence, because no sexual contact means no exposure"]
rationale: Other methods reduce risk, but abstinence removes it entirely.

stem: Sort each HIV statement as a myth or a fact.
options: ["Myth", "Fact"]
rows: ["HIV spreads through mosquito bites.", "Accurate facts help reduce stigma toward people with HIV.", "People can live long lives with HIV by taking treatment.", "HIV spreads through shared toilets."]
rationale: Accurate information reduces stigma and fear.

stem: Why does this curriculum call abstinence the most effective prevention method?
options: ["Because all other prevention methods have no effect at all on risk.", "Because it is the easiest option for every person to follow every day.", "Because it removes the risk of pregnancy and STIs, while others only reduce it.", "Because it matters for only one particular group of people in school."]
rationale: Abstinence is the only method with no risk; others reduce risk but do not eliminate it.

stem: Which statement about choosing abstinence is accurate?
options: ["It cannot be changed once someone has made the decision.", "It is only ever chosen for a single particular reason.", "It is a personal choice people can confirm at any time.", "It only counts if a person was never pressured by anyone."]
rationale: People choose abstinence for many reasons and can re-affirm the decision whenever they want.

stem: A fictional teen feels pressured. Match each statement to the decision-making step.
options: ["Identify the situation and values", "List options", "Weigh consequences", "Decide", "Reflect"]
rows: ["A friend wants me to do something that conflicts with my values", "I decide to say no and walk away", "Afterward I think about what went well and what to change", "Pressure may continue, but saying no keeps me true to my values and health", "I could say no, suggest another plan, leave, or call an adult"]
rationale: A decision-making model moves from the situation and values to options, consequences, a decision, and reflection.

stem: Which is a clear, respectful refusal that stays consistent with personal values?
options: ["\"Um, maybe, I don't know, it's complicated...\"", "\"No, that's not for me. Let's go.\"", "\"Wow, you're so immature for even asking that.\"", "\"I guess it is okay if you really want it.\""]
rationale: Clear, calm, and respectful language protects boundaries and the relationship.

stem: Which strategies help someone stay consistent with their values under pressure? Select all that apply.
options: ["Making excuses until the person stops asking", "Texting a trusted adult for help", "Agreeing to avoid being teased", "Walking away from the situation", "Practicing what to say before a pressure situation"]
rationale: Practice, exits, and support work better than excuses or giving in.

stem: Which are reliable resources for health information? Select all that apply.
options: ["A family doctor", "A site selling miracle cures", "A national health organization such as the CDC", "A school counselor or nurse", "A comment thread of strangers", "A county or city health department"]
rationale: Health professionals and recognized health organizations are reliable.

stem: A fictional classmate has a health question and is not sure whom to ask. Which two resources would you suggest?
options: ["The school nurse and a trusted doctor", "A quiz on a website that sells products", "Nobody at all, because they should handle it alone", "A comment thread of strangers and an ad"]
rationale: Reliable, accessible resources include the school nurse and a trusted doctor.

stem: Which statement about teen access to confidential health services is accurate?
options: ["Minors are never allowed to use any health service at all.", "Only parents can learn where to get health services.", "Rules vary by state, so a school nurse can explain local options.", "Services are always free and completely private for minors everywhere."]
rationale: Rules differ by state and provider; a nurse or counselor can explain what is available locally.

stem: Which are good first places to ask where to get testing or help? Select all that apply.
options: ["A school counselor", "A trusted doctor or clinic", "The school nurse", "The local health department", "A stranger in a comment section", "A friend's guess from social media"]
rationale: Professionals and public-health offices can give accurate local information.

stem: Which message to a friend is caring, accurate, and non-judgmental?
