options: ["\"You should feel embarrassed to ask about this stuff.\"", "\"People will talk if you ask, so keep quiet.\"", "\"Just search online; honestly it is not my problem.\"", "\"I'm here for you. A school nurse can help, and asking is okay.\""]
rationale: An effective message is caring, accurate, and free of shame.

stem: Jamal's blood pressure was a little high at one visit. Which statement about reading health metrics is most accurate?
options: ["Healthy ranges are identical for every person, whatever their age.", "A reading outside the usual range proves that the person is already sick.", "One number always shows the full picture of a person's overall health.", "One reading is a single data point, and trends over time matter too."]
rationale: Metrics are most useful when tracked over time and interpreted by a professional in context.

stem: Priya (fictional) often feels left out and has no one to talk to when school is hard. Which dimension of wellness is mostly affected?
options: ["Social wellness", "Financial wellness", "Environmental wellness", "Physical wellness"]
rationale: Having supportive relationships and someone to talk to are social wellness metrics.

stem: Which of these goals include all five SMART parts? Select all that apply.
options: ["Sleep 8 hours on school nights, Sunday to Thursday, for the next month to help focus in class.", "Drink 6 cups of water a day for two weeks to reduce afternoon headaches.", "Lose a lot of weight fast.", "Be less stressed."]
rationale: A SMART goal names a specific action, a measure, a realistic target, a reason, and a deadline.

stem: Which are warning signs that a health claim may be misleading? Select all that apply.
options: ["Uses only before-and-after photos and personal testimonials as proof", "Promises fast results with no effort, like \"lose 15 pounds in 10 days\"", "Cites a named study and links to it", "Sells a product while giving the advice", "Is reviewed by a medical organization"]
rationale: Quick-fix promises, testimonials instead of evidence, and a sales motive are common red flags.

stem: Lena is exhausted, has homework left, and friends want to hang out online. Which are realistic choices she could make? Select all that apply.
options: ["Tell her friends she will connect tomorrow", "Ignore everything and hope it works out", "Stay up all night doing both", "Play online for a short, set time, then stop and go to bed", "Finish homework, then go to bed on time"]
rationale: Good options are realistic and fit her responsibilities; ignoring the situation is not a choice that solves it.

stem: Sort each factor for a fictional teen as a risk factor or a protective factor.
options: ["Risk factor", "Protective factor"]
rows: ["Feeling close to family", "Being bullied at school", "Feeling connected to a school team or club", "Ongoing lack of sleep"]
rationale: Risk factors raise the chance of struggling; protective factors, like connectedness, help buffer stress.

stem: Why should a peer recognize and refer instead of trying to diagnose a friend?
options: ["A friend can diagnose a disorder after reading about it online.", "Warning signs only matter once a professional has diagnosed someone.", "Only professionals can diagnose, so friends notice and connect.", "Naming the exact disorder is the most helpful thing a friend can do."]
rationale: Peers notice and refer; diagnosing is for professionals.

stem: What happens in the body during the basic stress (fight-or-flight) response?
options: ["The body shuts down to rest until the stressor has passed.", "Heart rate and breathing speed up as the body prepares.", "Heart rate and breathing slow down so the body saves energy.", "Only the mind is affected by stress, never the body."]
rationale: The stress response activates the body, and recovery afterward is important.

stem: Sort each response to a struggling friend as supportive or dismissive.
options: ["Supportive", "Dismissive"]
rows: ["That sounds really difficult.", "Other people have it worse.", "I'm glad you told me.", "Just get over it."]
rationale: Supportive language validates feelings; dismissive language minimizes them.

stem: Which source is most likely to give credible mental-health information?
options: ["An influencer who earns money by selling a supplement", "A government health agency or medical group like the CDC", "An anonymous post written on a public online forum thread", "An ad promising a quick cure for stress and anxiety"]
rationale: Credible information comes from experts and evidence-based organizations.

stem: Clinics and grocery stores are nearby, but residents lack reliable transportation. Which intervention is the most realistic and best justified?
options: ["Expand a bus route to the clinic and grocery store, since transportation is the barrier.", "Build a second hospital in the area, even though one is already nearby.", "Open a luxury gym downtown, even though no one has asked for one.", "Tell residents to just walk farther, since distance is a personal matter."]
rationale: A good intervention targets the actual barrier identified in the scenario.

stem: Which best describes the difference between healthcare and public health?
options: ["Public health only responds to emergencies such as outbreaks.", "They mean the same thing, so the two terms can be swapped freely.", "Healthcare mainly treats individuals; public health protects whole populations.", "Public health treats individual patients in hospitals; healthcare protects populations."]
rationale: Healthcare focuses on individual patients, while public health works at the population level.

stem: Match each example to hazard, exposure, or risk.
options: ["Hazard", "Exposure", "Risk"]
rows: ["The chance of sunburn or skin damage", "Strong UV radiation from the midday sun", "Water contaminated with lead", "Working outside at noon without sunscreen"]
rationale: A hazard can cause harm, exposure is contact with it, and risk is the likelihood and severity of harm.

stem: An ad shows a smiling athlete holding a sugary drink but never states that it improves performance. What is the implied message?
options: ["That it is the cheapest drink available in the store", "That there is no message at all because no claim is stated", "That drinking it will make you athletic and successful", "That it is made with nothing but plain filtered water"]
rationale: Ads can communicate implied messages without making an explicit claim.

stem: Which is a clear call to action?
options: ["We ask the school board to approve filling stations by next semester.", "We hope that people will think more about hydration.", "Someone should really do something about water here soon.", "Water is important for the health of everyone at school."]
rationale: A call to action names who should do what and by when.

stem: Match each fictional example to tolerance, physical dependence, or addiction.
options: ["Tolerance", "Physical dependence", "Addiction (substance use disorder)"]
rows: ["The body adjusts so the same dose no longer works as well", "Needing larger amounts to get the same effect", "Continuing to use despite repeated harm and loss of control", "A patient takes prescribed pain medicine as directed and has withdrawal symptoms when it stops, with no compulsive use"]
rationale: Tolerance and physical dependence are body adaptations; addiction involves compulsive use despite harm, so they are not the same.

stem: Which are health risks linked to tobacco or vaping? Select all that apply.
options: ["Better focus in the long run", "Effects on attention and learning", "Improved lung capacity", "Nicotine addiction", "Irritation and harm to the lungs", "Cancer risk from toxic chemicals in burned tobacco"]
rationale: Nicotine, aerosol chemicals, and smoke are linked to addiction, lung harm, brain effects, and cancer.

stem: A fictional teen's ride home has been drinking. Match each statement to the decision-making step it shows.
options: ["Define the problem", "List options", "Think about consequences", "Choose the safest decision"]
rows: ["I could call a parent, find a sober driver, or stay overnight", "A crash could cause injury, legal trouble, and harm to others", "My ride has been drinking and I need to get home", "I will call a parent for a ride"]
rationale: A structured process moves from the problem to options, consequences, and the safest choice.

stem: A classmate offers a pill said to be "the same as a prescription one." Why can't that claim show the pill is safe?
options: ["Pills with natural-sounding ingredients are guaranteed to be safe.", "Pills sold for a low price are always the weaker versions.", "Pills that look like medicine always come from drug companies.", "Counterfeit pills can look real but contain fentanyl, so looks prove nothing."]
rationale: You cannot tell what is in a pill by looking, and counterfeit pills can be deadly.

stem: A fictional friend at a party is unresponsive after drinking. What is the best action?
options: ["Handle it alone so that no one else ever finds out", "Keep it secret to protect the friend from trouble", "Call for emergency help and get a trusted adult", "Wait until the morning to see how they are doing"]
rationale: Safety comes before secrecy; some situations need an adult or emergency help immediately.

stem: How does a seatbelt reduce the risk of serious injury in a crash?
options: ["It spreads crash force across the body and keeps you inside the vehicle.", "It only protects the driver, not the passengers in the car.", "It makes the car itself stop faster than it otherwise would.", "It prevents the crash from ever happening in the first place."]
rationale: Seatbelts reduce the force on the body and keep people inside the protective space of the vehicle.

stem: Which rhythm matches the recommended compression rate for hands-only CPR?
options: ["As fast as possible, about 180 compressions per minute", "Fast, then slow, then fast again in a repeating pattern", "A steady 100 to 120 compressions per minute", "A slow, careful pace of about 60 compressions per minute"]
rationale: A steady rate of 100 to 120 per minute keeps blood moving effectively.

stem: Myth: "Organ donation rules out an open-casket funeral." Which fact corrects it?
options: ["Donors cannot have any service.", "Donation always rules out a funeral.", "Donation does not prevent an open-casket funeral.", "Only some religions allow funerals after donation."]
rationale: Donation is performed with care and does not stop families from having a viewing or service.

stem: Match each example to the type of distraction it shows.
options: ["Visual", "Manual", "Cognitive"]
rows: ["Looking away from the road at a notification", "Reading a text while crossing a street", "Mind busy replaying an argument", "Taking a hand off the wheel to type"]
rationale: Distractions can take eyes, hands, or attention away from the task.

stem: How is MyPlate best described?
options: ["A list of foods that people should never eat", "A strict plan that every meal must match exactly", "A weight-loss diet that restricts certain foods", "A guide showing balance, not a strict rule"]
rationale: MyPlate shows balance across food groups rather than one perfect meal.

stem: Match each visual reference to what it can help estimate.
options: ["Palm", "Fist", "Cupped hand", "Thumb"]
rows: ["About one serving of meat or other protein", "About a serving of peanut butter or oil", "About a small handful-sized snack portion", "About a cup of cooked pasta or fruit"]
rationale: Hand-based references are a practical estimating tool, not a strict rule.

stem: Match each description to the FITT component.
options: ["Frequency", "Intensity", "Time", "Type"]
rows: ["How many minutes each session lasts", "How hard the body is working", "Walking, swimming, or strength training", "How many days per week"]
rationale: FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time, and Type.

stem: A snack bar front says "Made with real fruit!" but the label shows 18 g of added sugar. Which technique is this?
options: ["A health halo: a front claim hides the real label.", "A medical recommendation from a doctor or a dietitian", "Social proof, because many other buyers like the product", "A scarcity claim, because the bar seems to be a limited item"]
rationale: The front claim draws attention while the added sugar is on the full label.

stem: Which is a habit-based nutrition or activity goal?
options: ["Change my body shape to look like someone online.", "Stay under a set number of calories every single day.", "Add one serving of vegetables to dinner four nights this week.", "Lose 10 pounds by the end of June, whatever it takes."]
rationale: Habit-based goals focus on actions, not weight, calories, or body size.

stem: Which are signs of a reliable health website? Select all that apply.
options: ["It is run by a recognized health organization", "It has no author or sources", "It is mainly trying to sell a product", "It cites medical sources"]
rationale: Credible sources are run by experts, cite evidence, and are not mainly selling something.

stem: Sort each characteristic as healthy or unhealthy in a relationship.
options: ["Healthy", "Unhealthy"]
rows: ["Pressuring someone to do things they do not want to do", "Controlling who the other person can talk to", "Honesty and trust", "Respect for each other's opinions"]
rationale: Healthy relationships have respect, trust, and equality; control and pressure are unhealthy.

stem: Which statement about STIs is accurate?
options: ["All STIs can be cured with a short course of antibiotics.", "Only certain kinds of people can ever get an STI.", "STIs always cause symptoms that a person can easily see.", "Some are curable, some are manageable, and many show no symptoms."]
rationale: Many STIs have no symptoms, which is why testing matters for anyone who is sexually active.

stem: A fictional teen feels pressured. Match each statement to the decision-making step.
options: ["Identify the situation and values", "List options", "Weigh consequences", "Decide", "Reflect"]
rows: ["Pressure may continue, but saying no protects my values and health", "A partner is pressuring me, and I want to wait", "Later, I think about what worked and what I would do differently", "I will say no and suggest something else to do", "I can say no, change the subject, leave, or talk to a trusted adult"]
rationale: A decision-making model moves from the situation and values to options, consequences, a decision, and reflection.

stem: Which are good first places to ask where to get testing or help? Select all that apply.
options: ["Rumors in a group chat", "The school counselor", "A trusted doctor", "A social media influencer", "The school nurse", "The local health department"]
rationale: Professionals and public-health offices can give accurate local information.

stem: Priya's resting heart rate was a little high at one clinic visit. Which statement about health metrics is the most accurate?
options: ["Any number outside the usual range means the person has a disease.", "The healthy range is the same for toddlers, teens, and older adults.", "One reading gives a complete and final picture of a person's health.", "A single reading is a snapshot, and patterns over time matter."]
rationale: Metrics are best interpreted over time and with a health professional.

stem: Omar (fictional) feels overwhelmed and snaps at others when he is frustrated, even though he has good friends. Which dimension is mostly affected?
options: ["Financial wellness", "Emotional wellness", "Environmental wellness", "Physical wellness"]
rationale: Understanding and managing feelings is an emotional wellness skill.

stem: Which of these goals include all five SMART parts? Select all that apply.
options: ["Do a 10-minute breathing exercise every evening for two weeks to reduce stress.", "Get in shape somehow.", "Feel happier.", "Walk to school on 3 mornings a week for the next month to build energy."]
rationale: A SMART goal names an action, a measure, a realistic target, a reason, and a deadline.

stem: Which are warning signs that a health claim may be misleading? Select all that apply.
options: ["Was reviewed by independent health experts", "Names the study and links to the full report", "Is selling the very product it recommends", "Says a product will \"melt fat\" with no effort", "Relies on a single photo of one person as proof"]
rationale: Effortless miracle results, thin proof, and a sales motive are common red flags.

stem: Mateo is tired, has homework left, and friends want to chat online. Which are realistic choices he could make? Select all that apply.
options: ["Do nothing and hope it all works out", "Tell friends he can chat tomorrow after school", "Stay up all night trying to do everything", "Finish homework, then go to bed on time", "Join the chat briefly, then stop at a set time"]
rationale: Realistic options fit his responsibilities; ignoring the situation solves nothing.

stem: Sort each factor for a fictional teen as a risk factor or a protective factor.
options: ["Risk factor", "Protective factor"]
rows: ["A caring teacher or coach", "Being left out by classmates every day", "Constant conflict at home", "A routine with enough sleep and downtime"]
rationale: Risk factors raise the chance of struggling; protective factors help buffer stress.

stem: Why should a student refer a friend for help instead of diagnosing the friend?
options: ["Diagnosing a friend is the fastest way to solve the problem.", "Diagnosis takes professional training, so a peer can notice and refer.", "Peers can diagnose accurately by comparing symptoms to an online list.", "Warning signs are not important unless a doctor says so."]
rationale: Peers recognize and refer; diagnosing is for trained professionals.

stem: Which best describes what happens in the body during the stress response?
options: ["Heart rate drops so that energy is saved for later.", "Stress changes only thoughts and never affects the body.", "The body slows down so it can rest until the stress ends.", "The body speeds up heart rate and breathing to react."]
rationale: The stress response activates the body; recovery afterward matters.

stem: Sort each response to a struggling friend as supportive or dismissive.
options: ["Supportive", "Dismissive"]
rows: ["Just cheer up, it could be worse.", "Thanks for trusting me with this.", "You're making a big deal out of nothing.", "That sounds like a lot to deal with."]
rationale: Supportive language validates feelings; dismissive language minimizes them.

stem: Which source is most likely to provide credible mental-health information?
options: ["A video by a person who is promoting a paid online course", "A medical center or government health site such as NIMH", "A viral post from someone who has no medical credentials", "A website with ads that promise instant, guaranteed results"]
rationale: Credible information comes from experts and evidence-based organizations.

stem: Residents live near a clinic but have no safe way to get there at night. Which intervention is the most realistic and best justified?
options: ["Open a high-end spa near the clinic for residents to enjoy.", "Build a second clinic nearby, even though one is already close.", "Tell residents to travel at night despite any danger, since it is personal.", "Add better lighting and a night bus stop to make travel safe."]
rationale: A good intervention targets the actual barrier in the scenario.

stem: Which statement best explains how public health differs from healthcare?
options: ["Healthcare protects whole communities; public health treats individual patients.", "Public health only exists to respond to natural disasters.", "The two are identical and have the same goals and methods.", "Public health protects whole communities; healthcare mainly treats individuals."]
rationale: Public health works at the population level; healthcare focuses on individual patients.

stem: Match each example to hazard, exposure, or risk.
options: ["Hazard", "Exposure", "Risk"]
rows: ["Standing next to the speakers for hours", "The chance of permanent hearing loss", "Wildfire smoke drifting into town", "Loud speakers at a concert"]
rationale: A hazard can cause harm, exposure is contact with it, and risk is the likelihood and severity of harm.

stem: A cereal ad shows a happy family at breakfast but never states that the cereal is healthy. What is the implied message?
options: ["That it is made without any ingredients at all", "That it has the lowest sugar of any cereal", "That there is no message because no claim is stated", "That eating it leads to a happy family morning"]
rationale: Ads can imply benefits without making an explicit claim.

stem: Which is a clear call to action?
options: ["We hope that people will think more about sun safety.", "Shade is important for the health of everyone at the park.", "We ask the city to install shade structures at the park by next summer.", "Someone should really do something about the sun here soon."]
rationale: A call to action names who should do what and by when.

stem: Match each fictional example to tolerance, physical dependence, or addiction.
options: ["Tolerance", "Physical dependence", "Addiction (substance use disorder)"]
rows: ["A patient on prescribed medicine has withdrawal when it stops but no craving or compulsive use", "Needing a bigger dose over time to feel the same effect", "Using a substance compulsively despite damage to school and relationships", "Feeling sick and shaky when a medication is suddenly stopped"]
rationale: Tolerance and dependence are body adaptations; addiction is compulsive use despite harm.

stem: Which are health risks linked to tobacco or vaping? Select all that apply.
options: ["Higher risk of heart and lung disease over time", "Nicotine dependence", "Better sleep from nicotine", "Trouble with concentration and mood", "Stronger lungs from inhaling aerosol", "Coughing and airway irritation"]
rationale: Nicotine, aerosol, and smoke are linked to dependence, airway irritation, brain effects, and long-term disease.

stem: A fictional teen's driver has been drinking. Match each statement to the decision-making step it shows.
options: ["Define the problem", "List options", "Think about consequences", "Choose the safest decision"]
rows: ["I will call a family member to pick me up", "A crash could cause injuries, arrests, and lost trust", "I could call a family member, wait for a sober driver, or use a ride service", "A friend offers to drive me home after drinking"]
rationale: A structured process moves from the problem to options, consequences, and the safest choice.

stem: A fictional friend says a blue pill from a stranger is "just a pain pill." Why can't anyone tell it is safe by looking?
options: ["Real pills always carry a logo that proves they are genuine.", "Pills with natural-sounding ingredients are always safe to take.", "Fake pills can look real but contain fentanyl.", "Pills sold at a cheap price are always the weaker versions."]
rationale: You cannot tell what is in a pill by looking, and counterfeit pills can be deadly.

stem: A fictional teen finds a friend who took pills and is hard to wake. What is the best action?
options: ["Keep quiet so the friend avoids getting in trouble", "Wait to see if the friend feels better later", "Call 911 and get a trusted adult immediately", "Try to handle it alone so adults never find out"]
rationale: Safety comes before secrecy; some situations need emergency help immediately.

stem: How does a seat belt help protect you in a crash?
options: ["It keeps you from hitting the dashboard or leaving the car.", "It only helps in slow crashes under ten miles per hour.", "It makes crashes less likely by keeping the car steady.", "It protects the car's seat more than it protects the passenger."]
rationale: Seat belts hold people in place so crash forces are absorbed by stronger parts of the body.

stem: Which tempo fits the compression rate for hands-only CPR?
options: ["As fast as you possibly can, around 200 a minute", "A steady beat of 100 to 120 compressions a minute", "A slow, careful pace of about 40 compressions a minute", "Fast for a while, then a long pause, then fast again"]
rationale: A steady rate of 100 to 120 per minute keeps blood moving effectively.

stem: Myth: "You must be young and perfectly healthy to be an organ donor." Which fact corrects it?
options: ["Only people under twenty-five can ever become donors.", "People of many ages and health conditions can register as donors.", "Donors must pass a fitness test before they can sign up.", "Only people with no medical history at all can register."]
rationale: Age and many health conditions do not automatically rule out registering as a donor.

stem: Match each example to the type of distraction it shows.
options: ["Visual", "Manual", "Cognitive"]
rows: ["Holding a phone with one hand while steering", "Glancing at a map app instead of the road", "Watching a video on a screen while crossing a street", "Thinking about tomorrow's test while driving"]
rationale: Distractions can take eyes, hands, or attention away from the task.

stem: Which statement about MyPlate is accurate?
options: ["It shows balance and variety across food groups as a flexible guide.", "It requires every meal to match its picture exactly.", "It lists the only foods that people are allowed to eat.", "It is a calorie-restricted plan for losing weight."]
rationale: MyPlate shows balance across food groups rather than one perfect meal.

stem: Match each visual reference to what it can help estimate.

stem: A drink says "Real fruit juice!" on the front, but the label shows 24 g of added sugar. Which technique is this?

rationale: Habit-based goals focus on actions, not weight, calories, or body size.

stem: Which are signs of a reliable health website? Select all that apply.

stem: Sort each characteristic as healthy or unhealthy in a relationship.
